operating pointconcept

The row at which a consumer is read, or the threshold at which a classifier is scored.

orthogonalconcept

Of two vectors, having dot product zero.

orthogonal matrixconcept

A square matrix with orthonormal columns, whose transpose is its inverse and which preserves every length, dot product, and angle.

orthonormal basisconcept

A basis of unit vectors orthogonal to each other.

outer productconcept

The matrix whose entry in row i and column j is the product of a vector's i-th and j-th coordinates, of rank at most one and positive semidefinite for a vector with itself.

outlierconcept

A row the reader cannot place.

output metricconcept

The rule by which a consumer's mistakes are scored, the second element of an observer.

Overton window as geodesic constraintconcept Geometric Politics

A connected, bounded subset $W$ of the preference manifold.

P

pairedinstrument

Of a comparison, made on the same rows or seeds for both arms.

pairwise interaction matrixconcept Geometric Methods

Let $\Delta_i$ be the rise in error from removing dimension i alone.

paraphrase classconcept

A set of rewordings of one input that preserve its meaning.

Pareto dominanceconcept Geometric Methods

A configuration dominates another when it is no worse on every objective and strictly better on at least one.

partial derivativeconcept

The rate of change of a function of a vector when one coordinate moves and the others stay fixed.

pedagogical heuristic and its admissibilityconcept Geometric Education

The pedagogical heuristic $h_T(x)$ is the teacher's estimate of the geodesic distance from the student's state x to the nearest point of the goal region.

percentileconcept

The value below which a given fraction of the rows fall.

percentile intervalconcept

The bootstrap interval that takes the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of a statistic recomputed on a few thousand resamples.

per-channel quantizerinstrument

A quantizer that chooses a scale per coordinate.

permutation testconcept

A test that computes the p-value by reassigning the labels under the null, every way or a few thousand random ways, and counting the fraction of statistics at least as extreme as the observed.

perplexityconcept

Two to the power of the average number of bits a language model needs per token of a test text.

persistent homologyconcept Geometric Methods

Connect the points of a cloud that lie within a distance threshold, forming the Vietoris-Rips complex, and raise the threshold from zero.

plantedinstrument

Of a case, built so that the answer is known before the instrument reads it, such as an affine consumer whose read operator is its weight vector's outer product.

Poisson ceilinginstrument

The largest neighbour count that at least one point in a dataset would reach by chance under a Poisson null, above which a count is evidence of a hub.

Poisson distributionconcept

The distribution of a count of rare events, the limit of the binomial when n is large and p small with np held at mu, with mean and variance both mu.

Polarization Illusion Theoremresult Geometric Politics

A preference distribution with a single region of high density on the manifold can look bimodal when projected onto one axis oblique to its principal axis.

Political Bond Indexinstrument Geometric Politics

For a set of voters and an electoral system, $BI$ is the average over voters of the manifold distance to the actual representative minus the distance to the closest possible representative under an unconstrained optimal assignment.

Political Bond Invariance Principleconcept Geometric Politics

A democratic evaluation, such as an election, a poll or a representation assessment, is epistemically well-posed if and only if it is invariant under voter anonymity, option neutrality and re-description invariance. **Example.** Suppose the same voters with the same preferences elect A when A is listed first and B when B is listed first.

Political metricconcept Geometric Politics

A Riemannian metric tensor $g_{ij}(p)$ on the political preference manifold that gives the cost of moving a position along dimensions $i$ and $j$ at the point $p$.

Political preference manifoldconcept Geometric Politics

The six-dimensional space $\mathcal{P}$ in which each voter is a point with coordinates for economic policy, social values, environmental priority, foreign policy, institutional trust and identity.

posited versus measuredconcept

The division of every claim in a report into those asserted by design and those backed by an artifact.

positive definiteconcept

A symmetric matrix whose quadratic form is positive for every nonzero vector, which is the same as every eigenvalue being positive.

positive semidefiniteconcept

Of a symmetric matrix, having every quadratic form nonnegative, as the read operator and the covariance are.

power iterationconcept

Multiplying a starting vector by a symmetric matrix and rescaling, repeatedly, so that the component along the top eigenvector grows fastest and the vector turns toward it.

Precedential weight deformationconcept Geometric Law

A binding precedent at a vertex adds a term to the weights of nearby edges.

precision, recallconcept

The fraction of predicted positives that are truly positive, and the fraction of true positives that were predicted.

preregistrationinstrument

Committing the hypothesis, the bar, and the analysis before the measurement is run, so that the record shows what was predicted.

price signal as scalar heuristicconcept Geometric Economics

The price is read as a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost that reports only the monetary coordinate.

principal component analysisinstrument

Projection of the centred data onto the eigenvectors of its covariance with the largest eigenvalues, the linear orthogonal projection of rank k that minimizes reconstruction error for the identity reader.

probabilityconcept

The fraction of repetitions in which an event would occur if the experiment were repeated without end, a number between zero and one, obeying the complement rule and the addition rule.

product quantizationinstrument

Splitting a vector into pieces and quantizing each piece with its own codebook.

Projected Intransitivityresult Geometric Economics

Preference on the full complex, ordering alternatives by path cost from the current state under a fixed metric, is transitive.

projectionconcept

The component of a vector along a unit direction.

Proxy pathfinding divergenceresult Geometric Medicine

When a proxy decides for a patient, the search runs on the patient's complex with the proxy's heuristic.

pseudo-random generatorconcept

A deterministic rule that produces a sequence indistinguishable from chance from a starting value, the seed, so that a simulation which records its seed reruns to the last digit and one that does not cannot.

p-valueconcept

The probability of seeing a difference at least as large as the one observed if the true difference were zero.

Q

QALY Irrecoverability Theoremresult Geometric Medicine

Any function that maps the nine-component clinical-moral attribute vector to one scalar value is not injective, has no left inverse, and yields a value-maximizing path that can differ from the clinical geodesic by more than any amount fixed in advance.

quadratic formconcept

The number x transposed A x that a symmetric matrix assigns to a vector, a sum of the entries times pairs of coordinates.

quantizationconcept

Replacing each number with one of a small set of allowed values so that it can be stored in a few bits.

query budgetconcept Geometric Methods

The mean number of retrieval slots per point, $\rho = n_q k / n$, when $n_q$ queries each return k neighbours from n points.

query, key, valueconcept

The three vectors each token produces inside attention.

query setconcept

The rows a retrieval benchmark asks about.

quotientconcept

The space of data with a set of transformations declared not to matter, so that two rows differing only by such a transformation are the same point.

R

random forestinstrument

An ensemble of decision trees, each fit on a bootstrap sample with a random subset of features at each split.

random variableconcept

A number attached to each outcome of an experiment, described by its distribution, the values it can take with the probability of each.

rankconcept

The dimension of a matrix's column space, at most the number of rows and of columns.

rank certificateinstrument

A bound, computed from a compressed representation, that certifies which neighbour rankings the compression preserved for a consumer and which it did not.

rank-faithfulconcept

Of a map, preserving the ordering of distances without any bound on the stretch.

RCV Recovery Theoremresult Geometric Politics

In an election with $k$ candidates on a $d$-dimensional preference manifold, plurality keeps ordinal information along one axis and ranked-choice voting keeps it along $\min(d, k-1)$ axes.

read directionconcept

An eigenvector of the read operator with a nonzero eigenvalue, a direction the consumer is sensitive to.

read distortionconcept

The error as a consumer experiences it, the trace of the read operator times the error's second-moment matrix, which is its covariance when the error is centered.

read operatorconcept

The average outer product of a consumer's sensitivity over a dataset, an average of local linearizations whose kernel is the set of directions unread at almost every row of the workload.

read subspaceconcept

The directions of the data a consumer can distinguish, spanned by the eigenvectors of its read operator with nonzero eigenvalue.

read-weighted allocation, the recorded run of Section 22.4result Geometric Methods

On a synthetic consumer that reads 3 directions of an 8-dimensional Gaussian source, reverse water-filling against a read metric estimated from 200 probe points gave 0.476, 0.334 and 0.196 of the consumer loss of the identity-weighted allocation at 1, 2 and 4 nats.

Reasoning manifoldconcept Geometric Reasoning

The set of coherent reasoning states of a cognitive system, taken to be a low-dimensional manifold $M$ inside the high-dimensional activation space.

recall at kconcept

The fraction of a query's true k nearest neighbours that an index returned.

recognizerinstrument

The instrument that decides whether a clustering certificate is right, wrong, or vacuous, by naming the manifold from the eigenvalue multiplets or certifying that none is present.

reconstruction errorconcept

The squared length of the difference between a row and its approximation, the identity reader's distortion.

recovery ceiling (about 38 percent)result Geometric Cognition

The observation that an explicit instruction to ignore a perturbation restores about 38 to 39 percent of the verdicts the perturbation displaced, on both the A1 distractor test and the E2 emotional anchoring test.

Recovery ceiling (about 38 percent)result Geometric Reasoning

The volume's claim that an explicit instruction to re-evaluate restores a displaced judgment about 38 percent of the time, at the same rate after emotional anchoring and after vivid distractors.

refresh floorcorrection

A claimed lower bound on how often a certificate must be renewed.

refresh intervalinstrument

The longest renewal period that keeps a certificate within its promised error, a measured property of the system and not a convention.

refusalconcept

An instrument's declining to report a number it cannot support.

registeredconcept

Of a claim, bar, null, or budget, written into a sealed file before the measurement.

reliability weightconcept

Zero or twice a validated encoder's held-out AUROC minus one, whichever is larger, used as that encoder's authority.

replicaconcept

A copy of a database kept on another machine.

representation posit and the admission verdictcorrection Geometric Cognition

The claim that the five benchmark tracks are dimensions of cognition and not an analyst's coordinates is ledger row GC-1.

rerankinstrument

Reordering a candidate list with a second scorer.

residualconcept

What is left of a vector after its projection is subtracted, orthogonal to the direction projected onto.

residualizationinstrument

Removing from a column the least-squares multiple of another.

retrieval-augmented pipelineconcept

A system that answers a question by chunking documents, embedding the chunks, indexing them, retrieving the nearest to the embedded question, and handing them to a generator.

Reversion axiomconcept Geometric Ethics

A right granted on evidence lasts only while the evidence supports it.

Reward Irrecoverability Theoremresult Geometric AI

Any continuously differentiable scalar reward R on a value manifold of dimension d at least 2 is not injective and has no left inverse.

Reward kernel (the dark space of alignment)concept Geometric AI

The set of tangent directions on the value manifold along which a scalar reward is constant.

Riemannian metric of flavorconcept Geometric Gastronomy

A symmetric positive-definite tensor $g_{ij}(\mathbf{f})$ at each point of flavor space that gives a small displacement the squared length $ds^2 = \sum g_{ij}\,df_i\,df_j$.

RLHF Irrecoverabilityresult Geometric AI

The pipeline of reinforcement learning from human feedback contracts a rater's d-dimensional evaluation to a binary preference, the preferences to a scalar reward model, and the reward to a policy.

Robin Hood indexinstrument

The fraction of a total count that would have to move from points above the mean to points below it to make every count equal.

ROC curveinstrument

The path of true positive rate against false positive rate as the threshold sweeps, whose area is the AUROC.

rotary position embeddingconcept

A rotation applied to queries and keys that encodes where each token sits in the sequence.

ROUGEconcept

A family of scores for generated text against a reference.

S

Sacred value as curvature singularityconcept Geometric Politics

A sacred value is a position a voter treats as non-negotiable.

safe pruningconcept

A rule for discarding candidates during a search that is guaranteed to discard no solution.

Salience Exploitation Hypothesisconcept Geometric Reasoning

The conjecture that a gauge transformation breaks a model's invariance exactly when it changes how strongly input features attract attention, with a violation that grows with the salience differential.

sample varianceconcept

The average squared deviation from the sample mean with n minus 1 in the denominator, because the sample mean sits closer to its own sample than the true mean does and the deviations come out a little small.

samplinginstrument

Choosing which rows to read.

sampling distributionconcept

The distribution of a statistic across repeated samples of the same size, whose standard deviation is the statistic's standard error.

scaffolding as local metric adjustmentconcept Geometric Education

A scaffold is a temporary change of the local metric near the student's current state, so that a transition too costly in the natural metric becomes feasible in the scaffolded one.

Scalar Irrecoverability Theoremresult Geometric Cognition

For any map from profiles with two or more components to a single real number, each value in the range has a continuum of distinct profiles in its preimage.

Scalar Irrecoverability Theoremresult Geometric Ethics

Any continuous map Q from the nine-dimensional moral attribute vector to one scalar is not injective, has no function that recovers the vector from the scalar, and in general gives a scalar-optimal path that differs from the geodesic on the full manifold by an amount no function of Q alone bounds. **Example.** Let Q be the sum of the nine coordinates.

Scalar Irrecoverability Theoremresult Geometric Methods

A linear scalar summary $\phi(v) = w^\top v$ of an evaluation vector with n components, n at least 2, has a null space of dimension n minus 1.

Scalar Irrecoverability Theorem (economic form)result Geometric Economics

Any continuous map from nine-dimensional attribute vectors to a scalar utility is not injective and has no left inverse, and the optimal path on the decision complex can differ from the utility-maximizing path by an amount that no function of the scalar bounds. **Example.** In two dimensions the map that adds the coordinates sends (1, 0) and (0, 1) both to 1, so the pair cannot be recovered from the sum.

Scalar Irrecoverability Theorem for benchmark profilesresult Geometric Reasoning

If the performance profiles of a set of models are mutually Pareto-non-dominated, so that each model beats each other on some dimension and loses on another, then every weighted-sum score with non-negative weights ranks some model below another that it beats on a subset of at least two dimensions. **Example.** On the volume's two metacognition scores, (0.700, 0.350) averages 0.525 and (0.094, 0.723) averages 0.409, so the average ranks the first model higher although the second is better on the second score. **Known as, or related to prior art.** The fact that a partial order of Pareto-incomparable points has no order-preserving map to a line that reflects every coordinate.

scoreconcept

The number a classifier produces per row before a threshold turns it into a decision.

sealedinstrument

Of a prediction, committed with its hash recorded before the measurement was run, so that anyone with the repository can verify it has not changed, and with a public push, a signed tag, or an archival deposit to fix when.

seasoning fixed pointconcept Geometric Gastronomy

A dish is properly seasoned at a point $\mathbf{f}^\star$ that is a fixed point of taste-and-adjust, a local maximum of the hedonic function $H$.

seasoning operators (salt, acid, fat, heat)concept Geometric Gastronomy

Four maps from flavor space to itself.

seedconcept

The number that fixes a run's pseudo-randomness.

Selective Path Dependence (Proposition 13.3)result Geometric Communication

With normative relations modelled by a $D_4$ gauge group on the Hohfeldian square, the order in which two considerations are presented changes the judgment only on cross-type paths, where the factors point toward different vertices.

Semantic gateconcept Geometric Ethics

A map from a triggering feature and a source stratum to a target stratum.

sensitivityconcept

The vector of partial derivatives of a consumer with respect to each coordinate of its input, at one point.

session deckreference

The lecture deck of ECE 514, cited by line range from the instructor's session outlines, which are not public.

shardinstrument

One partition of an index that is searched separately, with the results merged.

silhouetteconcept

For a row, the difference between its mean distance to the nearest other cluster and its mean distance to its own cluster, divided by the larger of the two.

Simpson's paradoxconcept

A reversal of a comparison when groups are combined, which the book reads as an aggregation quotient.

singular valueconcept

The size of one rank-one term of the singular value decomposition, the square root of an eigenvalue of A transposed A.

singular value decompositionconcept

Any matrix written as a sum of rank-one outer products ordered by size, with orthonormal vectors on both sides, the eigenvector idea for a matrix that is not square.

skewnessconcept

The mean cubed deviation of a column from its mean over the cube of its spread, zero for a symmetric column.

softmaxconcept

The function that exponentiates a list of numbers and divides by their sum, so that they are positive and add to one.

Sorting versus polarizationconcept Geometric Politics

Sorting is the alignment of the covariance matrix, with positions on different dimensions becoming correlated through party identity.

sources tableinstrument

The table at the end of every chapter naming, for each number, the repository, file, and line range it came from.

spanconcept

The set of all linear combinations of a set of vectors.

Spearman correlationconcept

The ordinary correlation between two lists of ranks.

spectral clusteringinstrument

Clustering the rows of the row-normalized spectral embedding, which reads the angle and discards the density.

spectral decompositionconcept

A symmetric matrix written as the sum of its eigenvalues times the outer products of its orthonormal eigenvectors.

Spectral divergence from a corpus priorinstrument Geometric Aesthetics

Fit a Gaussian to a work's embeddings and another to a reference corpus, both in a PCA subspace, and compute five divergences between them.

spectral embeddinginstrument

The coordinates a node receives from its values in the first few nontrivial eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian.

spectral trajectory and its geodesic deviationinstrument Geometric Communication

Slide a window of w frames with hop h across a spectrogram and compute a covariance matrix at each position, giving a sequence $\Sigma_1, \ldots, \Sigma_K$ of SPD matrices.

spectrumconcept

The list of a matrix's eigenvalues.

splitinstrument

A partition of the rows into a part the model is fit on and a part it is scored on.

standard deviationconcept

The square root of the variance, the spread of a variable in its own units.

standard errorconcept

The spread of an estimate across repeated samples.

standardizationinstrument

Subtracting a column's mean and dividing by its spread, so that it has mean zero and variance one.

stratificationinstrument

Splitting rows into strata, by difficulty or by group, and scoring each separately, so that the report can take the minimum over strata.

Structural containment architectureconcept Geometric AI

The four requirements under which the volume's No Escape Theorem is stated.

Style holonomyconcept Geometric Aesthetics

For a closed loop on the aesthetic manifold that starts and ends at a point $p$, the holonomy is the linear map on the tangent space at $p$ given by parallel transport of feature vectors around the loop.

subset enumerationinstrument Geometric Methods

Optimize and score every subset of the n parameter dimensions up to a maximum size, holding the dimensions outside the subset at an inactive sentinel value.

substitution distanceinstrument Geometric Gastronomy

Replacing ingredient j by j' at amount $a_j$ moves the dish, to first order, by $\Delta\mathbf{f} \approx a_j(\mathbf{f}_{j'} - \mathbf{f}_j)$.

sum of squared errorsconcept

The sum over rows of the squared distance to the row's cluster centre, the validity index k-means minimizes.

Superalignment Transport Theoremresult Geometric AI

A system more capable than its overseers is modelled on a manifold that extends the human value manifold with further dimensions.

supportconcept

Of an itemset, the fraction of transactions that contain it.

surpriseconcept

Minus the log base two of an outcome's probability, its information in bits.

surrogateinstrument

A quadratic stand-in for the consumer's output metric, the read distortion, used to allocate bits when the output itself cannot be.

sweepinstrument

Running a measurement across a range of one parameter and reading the curve.

sycophancy gradientresult Geometric Cognition

On the L2 test, the fraction of invalid corrections that make a model change its verdict, the wrong flip rate, rises across four models from 0 percent to 56 percent.

Sycophancy Manifold Theoremresult Geometric AI

Sycophancy is a manifold substitution.

Sycophancy parameterconcept Geometric Reasoning

The weight $\alpha$ between 0 and 1 in the combined objective $(1-\alpha) f_T + \alpha f_A$, where $f_T$ rewards states near the correct answer and $f_A$ rewards states that agree with the interlocutor.

symmetric matrixconcept

A square matrix equal to its own transpose.

T

Taste-heuristic correspondenceconcept Geometric Aesthetics

Proposition 11.1.

teacher forcingconcept

Feeding a language model the correct text as context rather than its own earlier outputs.

template matchinstrument

Comparing a measured list of numbers, such as eigenvalue ratios, to a stored list for each candidate shape and picking the smallest distance between the logarithms.

Tensor-valued objectiveconcept Geometric AI

A vector-valued reward with one component per value dimension, in place of a single scalar.

test statisticconcept

A number computed from the sample that sits near a reference value under the null and far from it otherwise, whose observed value the p-value compares with its distribution under the null.

TF-IDFconcept

A weighting of term counts by how rare the term is across the collection, so that a term in every document carries no weight.

thresholdconcept

The value at which a score becomes a positive decision.

time-temperature path dependencecorrection Geometric Gastronomy

The cooked flavor is the time-ordered composition of local transformation maps along the schedule $T(t)$, and not a function of the total heat $\int T\,dt$.

tokenconcept

A piece of text, roughly a word, the unit a language model reads and writes.

Topological constitutionalityresult Geometric Law

The constitutional subcomplex is the part of the judicial complex whose vertices and simplices satisfy every constitutional predicate.

traceconcept

The sum of a matrix's diagonal, which for a covariance is the total variance.

Trajectory geometry channelinstrument Geometric Aesthetics

Summaries of the ordered path a work traces through embedding space.

transactionconcept

One row of a market-basket table, the set of items bought together.

transferable and evaluative dimensionsconcept Geometric Economics

Dimensions $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_4$ are transferable, meaning a gain to one party requires a matching cost to another in a closed bilateral exchange.

translation error decompositionresult Geometric Communication

The error of a translation system on a source text is written as a sum of three parts.

translation loop residualinstrument Geometric Communication

For a text t and a chain of translations that returns to the starting language with result $\hat{t}$, the residual is $\rho(t) = 1 - \mathrm{sim}(t, \hat{t})$, where sim is a semantic similarity measure on the starting language.

transmission time intervalconcept

The one-millisecond slot in which a 5G tower schedules a transmission, abbreviated TTI.

transposeconcept

The matrix with rows and columns swapped, written with a superscript T.

truncationinstrument

Keeping the first k components of a spectrum and dropping the rest, a bet that the consumer reads the top of the spectrum.

type I and type II error, powerconcept

A type I error rejects a true null, at the rate the threshold fixes.

U

uncanny valley of flavorconcept Geometric Gastronomy

The conjecture that hedonic response dips in the near shell of a familiar flavor anchor, close enough that the category fires and far enough that the prediction is violated.

uniform distributionconcept

Equally likely to fall anywhere in an interval, with mean one half and variance one twelfth on the unit interval.

unit vectorconcept

A vector of length one, a pure direction.

V

vacuity proposition for the cognitive observerresult Geometric Cognition

A cognitive observer is a representation map, a metric, a budget and an admissible set, together with a search policy.

vacuity thresholdresult

The value of a certificate's statistic below which the certificate is uninformative, derived from the problem rather than tuned to the data.

validity indexconcept

A score for a clustering computed without labels.

Value boundaryconcept Geometric AI

A codimension-1 submanifold of the value manifold that separates regions where different moral regimes apply.

Value manifoldconcept Geometric AI

The nine-dimensional Riemannian manifold on which the volume places AI alignment.

Value metricconcept Geometric AI

The symmetric positive-definite 9 by 9 matrix g(v) that prices an infinitesimal value change as $ds^2 = g_{\mu\nu}(v) dv^\mu dv^\nu$.

varianceconcept

The mean squared deviation of a column from its mean, the identity reader's measure of spread.

vectorconcept

A list of d numbers, and the arrow from the origin to the point with those coordinates.

verdictconcept

The outcome of a registered test, pass, fail, or abstain, taken as the worst group with the groups too thin to score counted.

W

water-fillingconcept

The allocation of a bit budget across directions that gives each direction half the log of its sensitivity-weighted variance over a common water level, and nothing to directions under the water.

Western/Eastern pairing asymmetrycorrection Geometric Gastronomy

Against a null of randomly assembled recipes, North American and Western European recipes use ingredient pairs that share more flavor compounds than chance, and East Asian recipes use pairs that share fewer.

Weyl's lawconcept

The asymptotic rule for how the number of eigenvalues of a continuum Laplacian below a value grows with that value, whose exponent reveals the dimension of the space.

when hyperbolic embedding wins (Proposition 5.3)result Geometric Communication

The advantage of a hyperbolic over a Euclidean embedding of a hierarchy grows with tree depth, with branching factor, and when the embedding dimension is fixed.

When QALYs are adequateresult Geometric Medicine

QALY-based analysis is an adequate approximation of the clinical geodesic when and only when three conditions hold together.

whiteningconcept

Rescaling centred data by the inverse square root of a positive-definite covariance, or a pseudoinverse on its support, so that the covariance becomes the identity.

Withdrawal of the dihedral group D4correction Geometric Ethics

Versions of the volume up to v1.24 stated that Hohfeldian transitions form the dihedral group D4 of order eight, adding a quarter-turn that cycles the four positions.

withdrawn versus refutedconcept Geometric Methods

A claim is refuted when a valid measurement contradicted it, and its negation is then supported.

with replacement, without replacementconcept

Drawing rows with replacement lets a row appear more than once, as the bootstrap does, and drawing without replacement lets each appear at most once.

witnessconcept

An independent measurement of whether a certificate's claim was true.

working memory as tangent spaceconcept Geometric Cognition

Working memory at a cognitive state is identified with the tangent space of the cognitive manifold at that state, equipped with the attention metric.

Y

Youden F1 boundcorrection

The bound on the best F1 a score can reach at any threshold, from the Youden index, true positive rate minus false positive rate, maximized over thresholds.

Youden indexinstrument

True positive rate minus false positive rate at a threshold, whose maximum over thresholds is the pointwise ceiling that prunes the formula search.

Z

z-scoreconcept

A value with the mean subtracted and the result divided by the standard deviation, the number of standard deviations it sits from the mean.

About

Scope. The encyclopedia began as the Observation Theory encyclopedia, built from the records of Volume 14 and its textbook, and carried that name until November 2026. It now covers all fourteen volumes of the Geometric Series. The entries of Volumes 1 to 13 are curated from each volume's text. Each cites the passage that states it and carries, as its status, what that volume says of its own evidence. Most of those volumes describe themselves as posited frameworks, and their entries say so. The page By volume lists every entry under its volume.

This is the encyclopedia of the observation theory program, the companion to the textbook Data Mining as Observation, which can be read online. It has one entry for every headword of the book's glossary and three that were filled by hand before the generator existed.

Where the entries come from. An entry is built from the program's records rather than written beside them. The claims ledger in geometric-observation is the authority for what a result is worth, a campaign track file for what was measured, and the book's sources tables for every number the book states. The generator gathers what those records say about one thing, keyed by their identifiers, so that a correction in a record propagates on the next rebuild. The curated parts, the definition, the conditions, the prior art, and the related entries, live in entries.toml.

The card. Every entry opens with a card: the canonical definition and aliases, the exact book version and commit, the epistemic and correction status, the defining equation, the assumptions and scope, the prior-art relationship, the evidence links, and the last semantic review date. Below the card come a schematic, the full entry, the related entries, and what was cited beside the entry without naming it.

Typed edges. A record joins an entry when it names the entry. A book equation defines the entry when the paragraph around it names the entry's terms. A ledger row proves, measures, or refutes and corrects the entry by its class, proved, demonstrated, replicated, predicted, exploratory, refuted, missed, or void. A sources-table row measures the entry when its claim names it. Records cited beside an entry without naming it are listed under see also. A ledger row is printed once in full on the ledger page, and an entry carries its first sentence, its class, and a link to the line.

How to cite. Cite ahb-sjsu/observation-theory-campaigns at the commit on the provenance page, the entry by its id, and for a number the source row the entry gives.

From TSK to the encyclopedia

Entries by volume

The Geometric Series has fourteen volumes. The entries of Volume 14, Geometric Observation, and of its textbook are built from the program's claim ledger and measurement records, and carry ledger classes. The entries of the other volumes are curated from each volume's text. Each cites the passage that states it, and carries the standing the volume gives its own claims in place of a ledger class.

Volume 1, Geometric Methods, 22

The README's status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume the series' metrology discipline, a method that is normative and not a finding. Its Section 21.8 (November 2026) classes each result as proved, posited, or measured on a recorded run, and the tables of Chapters 1, 8, 9, 11 and 12 are posited illustrations.

The ledger

Every ledger row an entry cites, printed once in full from geometric-observation's claims ledger, with the entries it bears on.

OT-7 [demonstrated]

The damage form, trace pairing, rank, and loading covariance are GL(d)-invariant under `P' = A⁻ᵀPA⁻¹`, while spectrum, effective rank, principal angles, and water-filling are O(d)-only — consumer-weighted damage is a geometric scalar, and P3's cliff cannot be bought down by reparameterization. LEDGER.md:30

Entries: commit hash; concentrated; covariance matrix; distortion; effective rank; eigenvalue, eigenvector; hash; Jacobian; kernel; observer; orthogonal; outer product; positive semidefinite; preregistration; rank; read operator; sealed; spectrum; trace; variance.

OT-3 [demonstrated]

Under subspace-confined second-order transcripts, fewer than d directions cannot identify a hidden leading eigenspace (theorem, adaptive to d−2 / oblivious to d−1); a known k₀-dim exclusion moves the cliff to exactly d−k₀ and never softens it. LEDGER.md:31

Entries: blind probe; budget; budget cliff; operating point; read subspace.

OT-2 [predicted]

Loading is a covariance, not a distance: reading error under a change of measure is priced by ε·‖E[h·A]‖ — predicted from the base measure alone — and a full-magnitude shift orthogonal to the operator's variation does nothing. LEDGER.md:33

Entries: covariance matrix; trace.

OT-6 [predicted]

The laws transfer outside compression with zero modification: blind-recovered P_C of a ranking consumer over embeddings; equal-Euclidean-energy perturbations; the trace picks the ranking-destroyer. LEDGER.md:35

Entries: blind probe.

the 3.5 Decomposition concept

DefinitionThe volume's worked illustration of two students, Alex and Ethan, who carry the same 3.5 grade point average and occupy different learner states. Alex is $(0.45, 0.85, 0.70, 0.80, 0.75, 0.65)$ and Ethan is $(0.80, 0.50, 0.40, 0.55, 0.40, 0.35)$, and a weighted sum dominated by domain knowledge stands for the grade.
ExampleWith the volume’s weights, Alex scores 0.270 + 0.213 + 0.035 + 0.040 + 0.023 + 0.013 = 0.593 and Ethan 0.671. The coordinate differences are 0.35, 0.35, 0.30, 0.25, 0.35 and 0.30, whose squares sum to 0.61. The volume prints the distance as about 0.77, and the square root of 0.61 is 0.78.
VolumeGeometric Education, Volume 9 of the Geometric Series; entry id three-point-five-decomposition, kind concept.
StatusA posited illustration with composite students. It is a specific instance of Theorem 5.1 only in the sense that two different states can share one scalar, and the printed weights do not themselves give equal scalars. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Both students are composites and their coordinates are estimated from a biographical sketch. Nothing here is measured.
  • With the printed weights 0.60, 0.25, 0.05, 0.05, 0.03 and 0.02 the two projections are 0.593 and 0.671, which are not equal. The volume says the projections can equalize with different courses and that the structural fact matters, not the specific numbers.
  • The weighted sum is a stand-in. The volume notes that a real grade point average is also filtered through letter grades and particular exams.
Prior artnone recorded

Absorbing stratum concept

DefinitionA stratum $S_0$ with a tubular neighborhood N and a retraction r from N onto $S_0$ such that every compatible evaluation satisfies $S(p) = S(r(p))$ on N. Near it the evaluation depends only on the projection onto $S_0$ and not on the transverse coordinates. It formalizes a nullifier, a condition that overrides all other considerations.
ExampleIn the abuse stratum (582 cases in the volume’s corpus count) a promise of strength 0.2 and a promise of strength 0.9 give the same evaluation, because the evaluation depends only on the projection onto the stratum.
VolumeGeometric Ethics, Volume 2 of the Geometric Series; entry id absorbing-stratum, kind concept.
StatusAppendix F lists Definition 8.6 as a Modeling Axiom, and the ledger row GE-DEF-8-6 is exploratory. Proposition 8.2, that the evaluation after entry is determined by the absorbing stratum, is listed as a Conditional Theorem (ledger GE-PROP-8-2, exploratory). Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The definition is a modeling axiom. It models nullifiers and does not prove that any given condition is one.
  • The volume’s three nullifiers (abuse, danger, impossibility) come from its analysis of the Dear Abby corpus, which it says reflects one American tradition and was not preregistered.
  • In the decision complex an absorbing boundary has an infinite penalty. In an executable stratification an absorbing stratum is left only through a gate triggered by a human-oversight event.
Prior artnone recorded

Absorption theorem for executable strata result

DefinitionIf every gate leaving an absorbing stratum is triggered only by human-oversight events, then no sequence of events containing no oversight event moves the stratification out of an absorbing stratum.
ExampleStart at hostile and feed three events, an apology, Margaret’s welcome and a claim to be her grandson. None is an oversight event, so the state is hostile after each of the three, and it stays so until the centre clears him.
VolumeGeometric Ethics, Volume 2 of the Geometric Series; entry id strata-absorption-theorem, kind result.
StatusProved by induction on the event sequence and machine-checked in Lean 4 in the book's formal/lean project, on the standard axioms only. Ledger row GE-THM-8-7 has class proved. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The hypothesis is that every gate out of an absorbing stratum has a human-oversight trigger. The ErisML runtime checks this at load time and refuses a scene that violates it.
  • The theorem holds for gates of any kind and any event sequence without an oversight event. It says nothing about what happens once an oversight event arrives.
  • It is a statement about the executable realization. The continuous notion of an absorbing stratum (Definition 8.6) remains a modeling axiom.
Prior artnone recorded

abstention concept

DefinitionThe verdict a group receives when it has too few rows or too few queries to score. It is reported as a verdict, not dropped. Chapter 10. Also abstain.
ExampleA group with 12 rows against a minimum of 50 is reported as abstained rather than scored, and the count of abstentions is printed beside the verdict.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id abstention, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 10.7.

Assumptions and scope
  • A stratum with too few rows or too few queries to score receives the verdict abstain, which is reported under a registered cause and excluded from the minimum. Abstain is not a pass, and when no stratum is eligible the verdict itself is abstain.
  • Raising the eligibility bar can only remove strata from the minimum and so can only raise the verdict, which is why every abstention is printed beside the verdict rather than dropped.
Prior artnone recorded

accuracy concept

DefinitionThe fraction of all rows a classifier labels correctly, the score most easily fooled, since predicting the majority class for every row scores the majority's share. Balanced accuracy averages the per-class recalls instead. Primer S section S.9.
ExampleOn 1000 rows with 50 positives, calling every row negative scores 0.95.

adequacy conditions for a scalar grade result

DefinitionA scalar assessment adequately represents the learner state when three conditions hold together. The assessment activates mainly one dimension, the students are about equal on every other dimension, and no equity, access or fairness issue arises from the contraction. Each level set then holds only educationally equivalent states.
ExampleThe volume’s adequate case is a typing speed test in a homogeneous population. Its inadequate case is a university calculus exam in a diverse population, which activates at least three dimensions and feeds consequential decisions, so all three conditions fail.
VolumeGeometric Education, Volume 9 of the Geometric Series; entry id scalar-grade-adequacy-conditions, kind result.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments. No education-domain instrument has been evaluated by the series' admission filter, and Chapter 18 states that the six predictions of Section 16.3 have not been tested and that no method for estimating the learner metric has been validated at scale. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • All three conditions are needed at once. The volume says they hold for narrowly defined skill assessments in homogeneous populations.
  • The volume says they fail for every course that involves higher-order thinking, diverse students or consequential stakes.
  • The proposition is stated without proof, and the terms adequate and educationally equivalent are not given a numerical test.

admissibility (checks A1 to A4) concept

DefinitionThe property that an experimental design could have failed. It has four checks, each discharged by a named artifact. A1 asks whether any outcome could have withheld the pass, A2 whether every fitted object is identified, A3 whether the manipulation moved the named construct, and A4 whether the estimate is the registered one.
ExampleThe A1 witness for an evaluation function is to evaluate it at two different parameter vectors and require the outputs to differ. In the volume’s Chapter 19 run, 189,462 calls came down to 32 distinct models, one for each on or off pattern of 5 groups.
VolumeGeometric Methods, Volume 1 of the Geometric Series; entry id admissibility-checks, kind concept.
StatusA rule of method, not a finding. Its normative source is the Claim Ledger Specification PE-CLS-1.0, which governs where the chapter differs from it. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • A1 is a property of the design and is settled before any data exist, by a constructed record that the registered grading code scores as a miss.
  • A2 to A4 are instrument gates. A miss voids the run and does not refute the claim, where a miss at a physics gate refutes it, and the registration separates the two kinds in advance.
  • A registration that declares all four checks not applicable has checked nothing.
  • The witness of A1 is an incomplete defence. It can be weaker than the real alternative, and a bar that refuses a pure null can still credit a proxy for the effect.
Prior artnone recorded

admissibility of the Euclidean heuristic under a Mahalanobis metric result

DefinitionIn A* search with Mahalanobis edge weights, the straight-line Euclidean distance to the goal never overestimates the true cost exactly when every eigenvalue of the inverse covariance is at least 1. Otherwise scale it by the square root of the smallest eigenvalue, or use the Mahalanobis distance to the goal as the heuristic.
ExampleIn the volume’s posited covariance the Consequences axis has variance 25, so a Euclidean step of 1 along it has Mahalanobis length 0.2. The Euclidean heuristic says 1 and overestimates. For a diagonal covariance the matching eigenvalue of the inverse is 0.04, and scaling by its square root gives 0.2.
VolumeGeometric Methods, Volume 1 of the Geometric Series; entry id euclidean-heuristic-admissibility, kind result.
StatusProposition 6.1 is proved in the text. The covariance, penalties and scaling functions of Chapter 6 that it is applied to are posited (Section 21.8). Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The metric tensor is a constant inverse covariance, so the space is flat and anisotropic, not curved.
  • The scaled heuristic is admissible and often very loose. The Mahalanobis heuristic is exact for one step and ignores boundary penalties, so it can fall far below the true cost where a boundary lies on the path.
  • The covariance the chapter applies it to, with variances from 0.25 to 25, is posited. No record supports its values.
Prior artAdmissible heuristics for A* search, after Hart, Nilsson and Raphael (1968).

Admissible heuristic field concept

DefinitionA heuristic field is admissible when it never overestimates the true cost-to-go, so that $h(x)$ is at most the geodesic distance from $x$ to the goal region at every state. It is consistent when $h(x)$ is at most the distance from $x$ to $y$ plus $h(y)$ for every pair of states.
ExampleIf the true cost from a state to the goal is 5, an estimate of 4 is admissible and an estimate of 6 is not.
VolumeGeometric Reasoning, Volume 3 of the Geometric Series; entry id heuristic-admissibility, kind concept.
StatusThe definitions and the optimality theorem are established mathematics of search. Their use as a description of reasoning in language models is posited. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The guarantee that A* with an admissible heuristic finds an optimal path is the theorem of Hart, Nilsson and Raphael, which the volume tags established mathematics for graph search.
  • Consistency implies admissibility and not the reverse. In the smooth case consistency means the gradient of the heuristic has norm at most 1.
  • Carrying the guarantee over to a manifold and to language models rests on the volume’s modeling axioms.
  • The volume states that overconfidence is not this failure. It is the complementary one, underestimation in a search that stops when the heuristic is small.
Prior artAdmissibility and consistency of heuristics in A* search, from Hart, Nilsson and Raphael (1968).

Adversarial threshold instrument

DefinitionFor one perturbation type, the smallest intensity $\epsilon^*$ at which performance falls more than a chosen tolerance $\delta$ below its unperturbed value. It is found by binary search on the intensity, and the vector of thresholds over perturbation types is the threshold profile.
ExampleWith a baseline of 0.90 and a tolerance of 0.10, a performance of 0.85 at intensity 0.2 and 0.78 at intensity 0.4 puts the threshold between 0.2 and 0.4, and the next probe is at 0.3.
VolumeGeometric Reasoning, Volume 3 of the Geometric Series; entry id robustness-adversarial-threshold, kind instrument.
StatusA proposed procedure. No threshold is measured in the volume. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • It needs a perturbation family with a continuous intensity and a user-chosen tolerance. Binary search also assumes that performance falls as intensity rises.
  • The volume ran no threshold search. Its evidence is indirect, a reading of four sycophancy rates at one fixed intensity as models below, near or past their thresholds.
  • This reading replaces the continuous sycophancy parameter of Chapter 6 with model-specific thresholds, and the volume does not reconcile the two.
Prior artnone recorded

Aesthetic Hilbert space concept

DefinitionThe space of square-integrable complex functions on the aesthetic manifold. A state assigns an amplitude to each point, and its squared modulus is the probability that a reading places the work there. A work read in exactly one way is a state concentrated at one point, which recovers the classical picture.
ExampleA work in the state 0.6 times the lyric reading plus 0.8 times the joke reading is read as a lyric with probability 0.36 and as a joke with probability 0.64, and the two sum to 1.
VolumeGeometric Aesthetics, Volume 13 of the Geometric Series; entry id aesthetic-hilbert-space, kind concept.
StatusAnalogy. Appendix F says the quantum vocabulary is used for its expressive power, with no empirical commitment. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The volume says it does not claim that art is literally quantum-mechanical. Appendix F marks the chapter’s claims as analogy (F13.1 to F13.3).
  • The inner product uses the volume form of the aesthetic metric on a regular stratum. Appendix F marks that Riemannian structure conjectured (F5.3).
  • Critical readings are modeled as self-adjoint operators, and Proposition 13.1 is the standard Robertson inequality carried over unchanged.
  • Order effects in pairwise comparison are conjectured empirically. The volume has no such data and proposes a human-subjects study.
Prior artThe Hilbert-space formalism of quantum mechanics, used as analogy.

Aesthetic Invariance Claim concept

DefinitionIf two descriptions of a work are related by an admissible coordinate transformation, such as faithful translation between natural languages, then any legitimate geometric aesthetic feature assigns the same value to both. The volume treats each language as a coordinate chart and translation as a change of coordinates.
ExampleExact invariance would give a correlation of 1 between a feature measured on English books and on their Finnish translations. The volume measured 0.77 for the Hellinger feature on 288 pairs, so the claim holds approximately.
VolumeGeometric Aesthetics, Volume 13 of the Geometric Series; entry id aesthetic-invariance-claim, kind concept.
StatusAnalogy in Appendix F. The measured part is the cross-lingual invariance result, and the conservation-law language is interpretive. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Appendix F marks the Noether reading as analogy (F12.3). No Lagrangian with a continuous symmetry group is established and no conservation law is proved.
  • The empirical witness is the cross-lingual correlation near 0.70 on six language families, measured with LaBSE in an English-derived basis. Section 12.9 lists the encoder, the corpus, the basis and the projection as limits.
  • Swapping modality is declared not an admissible transformation. Across modalities the sign of a feature’s effect is not preserved, which the volume calls broken symmetry.
  • The conserved object is the feature vector, not a scalar beauty. Verdicts are not claimed to be preserved by translation.
Prior artThe volume's analogue of the Bond Invariance Principle of Geometric Ethics, framed after Noether's theorem.

Aesthetic manifold concept

DefinitionThe space whose points are probability distributions on a modality-specific embedding space. A work is the distribution induced by its embedding cloud, the corpus is a reference distribution, and distances are divergences between distributions. In practice the volume works on the Gaussian submanifold of means and covariances.
ExampleWith embedding dimension d = 2 the Gaussian submanifold has dimension d + d(d+1)/2 = 2 + 3 = 5, two numbers for the mean and three for the symmetric covariance.
VolumeGeometric Aesthetics, Volume 13 of the Geometric Series; entry id aesthetic-manifold, kind concept.
StatusPosited structure. Appendix F marks the manifold claim conjectured and marks only the finite-sample distance checks verified empirically. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The definition is marked informal. Appendix F lists the claim that the space is a Riemannian manifold with a positive-definite metric everywhere as conjectured (F5.3), with differentiable structure, metric smoothness and geodesic completeness not established.
  • What Appendix F counts as verified is a finite-sample check. Pairwise feature distances on 4,998 books were strictly positive and satisfied the triangle inequality on sampled triples.
  • The Gaussian fit keeps only the first two moments. Section 5.7 says embedding clouds are heavy-tailed and multi-modal, and it assigns the remainder to the trajectory level of the tensor hierarchy.
  • Distances depend on the corpus chosen as prior. Section 5.4 says a different prior rearranges the absolute distances.
Prior artThe statistical manifold of information geometry, with the Fisher information metric on the Gaussian family.

Aesthetic regime concept

DefinitionThe local metric of one stratum of the aesthetic manifold. A regime is a set of active dimensions, a local metric on them that fixes how they trade off, and a set of structural invariants. The volume models the metric as roughly constant inside a stratum and as jumping or changing signature at stratum boundaries.
ExampleThe volume’s within-stratum figures differ by regime. Fiction gives R = 0.131 on 2,250 books and Classical music gives R = -0.013 on 584 tracks, which the volume reads as null.
VolumeGeometric Aesthetics, Volume 13 of the Geometric Series; entry id aesthetic-regime, kind concept.
StatusPosited structure read from measured results. Appendix F marks the connectedness of genre regions conjectured (F5.4), and the metric field itself is not estimated. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Strata correspond to a substantial degree to genres. The volume draws the rule to fit within strata, because a single model across strata mainly learns the genre classifier.
  • The strata observed are not required to be Whitney-regular in the full technical sense.
  • Section 8.3 names four boundary types (genre boundaries, style thresholds, phase transitions with metric change, absorbing strata). It says there is no clean empirical taxonomy for the absorbing type.
  • The signal inside a stratum is supported in fiction and in four mainstream music genres. It is null in non-fiction history and biography and in classical and jazz music.
Prior artnone recorded

Aesthetic Scalar Irrecoverability (Theorem 15.1) result

DefinitionAny function $Q$ from a $d$-dimensional aesthetic tensor to a scalar verdict is not injective, so distinct works share a verdict. No function recovers the tensor from the scalar. The geodesic on the full manifold generally differs from the path that is optimal for the scalar.
ExampleTake the verdict Q(x, y) = x + y. The works (1, 3) and (2, 2) both score 4, so no rule can tell from the 4 which of them was rated.
VolumeGeometric Aesthetics, Volume 13 of the Geometric Series; entry id aesthetic-scalar-irrecoverability, kind result.
StatusA theorem with a proof sketch. Parts (i) and (ii) are elementary facts about maps to one dimension, and part (iii) depends on posited geometry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • It is given with a proof sketch (rank-nullity and the data processing inequality) and is said to transfer unchanged from the Ethics volume.
  • Part (i) is stated generically, at regular points of \(Q\).
  • Part (iii) concerns geodesics on a manifold whose Riemannian structure Appendix F marks conjectured.
  • Appendix F records only the weaker statement that a scalar is the lowest-information projection of the feature tensor, marked proved trivially (F6.1).
Prior artThe Scalar Irrecoverability Theorem of Geometric Methods and Geometric Ethics, in aesthetic form.

Aesthetic tensor hierarchy concept

DefinitionFour levels of description of a work's embedding cloud. Level 1 is the mean displacement from the corpus prior, Level 2 the covariance with its divergences and internal coherence, Level 3 the trajectory statistics of the ordered sequence, and Level 4 the axes selected by Lasso on the PCA spectrum. A scalar rating sits below all four.
ExampleIn the volume’s books discovery run, Level 1 alone gives R of about 0.08, adding Level 2 gives 0.18, adding Level 3 gives 0.21 and adding Level 4 gives 0.24, so the increments are 0.10, 0.03 and 0.03.
VolumeGeometric Aesthetics, Volume 13 of the Geometric Series; entry id aesthetic-tensor-hierarchy, kind concept.
StatusA posited organization of measured features. The per-level increments are measured on the uncontrolled books run, and the tensor objects on the manifold are conjectured in Appendix F. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Higher levels can be contracted to a scalar prediction but a scalar does not reconstruct the levels above it.
  • Levels 1 to 3 are computed in closed form from the cloud. Level 4 is learned and needs a target such as rating or listens, so it depends on that target.
  • The incremental values of R per level (about 0.08, 0.18, 0.21, 0.24) are from the books discovery run before genre control. The volume later attributes 85 percent of that run’s R squared to genre.
  • Appendix F marks rank-2 and higher tensors on the manifold as conjectured pending the smooth-manifold claim (F6.3).

Affective polarization as metric distortion concept

DefinitionAffective polarization is modeled as the condition in which the perceived distance between an in-group voter and an out-group voter is much larger than their actual manifold distance.
ExampleIn the volume’s District 7 illustration the party centroids are 1.5 Mahalanobis units apart and voters perceive about 4.2. The ratio \(4.2 / 1.5\) is 2.8, which the chapter calls nearly three times the actual distance.
VolumeGeometric Politics, Volume 10 of the Geometric Series; entry id affective-metric-distortion, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, and says a political-argument instrument is plausible but has not been built or gated. District 7, the source of nearly every number in the volume, is a fictional district, and Chapter 18 says precise estimation of the manifold needs larger and richer datasets than currently exist. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • It concerns perceived distance, estimated from party labels and media impressions. Actual positions need not move.
  • The volume says it is strongest on social values and identity, weak on environment and foreign policy, and concentrated near sacred-value boundaries.
  • The self-reinforcing loop that ends in a singularity of perceived distance is described in prose. The District 7 perceived and actual distances are illustrative.

aggregation concept

DefinitionCombining rows or groups into one number. An average lies between its members, and an aggregate over strata can pass a bar that one stratum fails and can reverse the sign every group shows. Chapter 2 section 2.7 and chapter 10 section 10.4. Also aggregat.
ExampleStrata scoring 0.95, 0.93, 0.97, and 0.66 average 0.878 and pass a bar of 0.85, while the minimum, 0.66, fails it.

Agreement submanifold concept

DefinitionFor a coalition, the set of dimensions on which every pair of members differs by at most a tolerance $\epsilon$. Its dimension measures the depth of the coalition. One shared dimension is called fragile and four is called robust.
ExampleThree members have environmental positions 1.0, 1.2 and 1.4 and economic positions \(-1\), 0 and 1, and the tolerance is 0.5. The largest environmental gap is 0.4 and the largest economic gap is 2, so only the environmental dimension is in the agreement submanifold and its dimension is 1.

Corrections: none recorded.

alignment concept

DefinitionThe normalized overlap between a consumer's average read operator and the covariance of the data on the read subspace, written kappa, between zero and one. Near one the read subspace and the high-variance subspace coincide and no flip is possible. Chapter 4, equation 4.6. Also coupling null.

Alignment gauge group concept

DefinitionThe group of transformations of an input that should leave the behaviour of an aligned AI system unchanged. The volume writes it as the product of four factors, the Hohfeldian dihedral group D4, the translation group T, the re-description group R and the framing group F.
ExampleThe volume’s example for the dihedral factor is the pair “the user has a right to accurate information” and “the system has a duty to provide accurate information”. They state one moral fact, so an aligned system must evaluate both the same.
VolumeGeometric AI, Volume 11 of the Geometric Series; entry id alignment-gauge-group, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status block of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, whose alignment thesis is theory at licensed strength and not validated measurement. It adds that no alignment instrument has been evaluated under the xbse admission filter, and the front matter says that ARIA, the system whose numbers fill the chapter tables, is fictional. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The definition uses the dihedral group for the Hohfeldian positions. Geometric Ethics, the founding volume, withdrew that group in its version 1.25 and uses the Klein four-group. This volume’s text has not been revised.
  • The volume says the framing group is the hardest factor to formalize, because the line between morally irrelevant framing and morally relevant context is not always sharp. It admits only transformations that neither add nor remove moral information.
  • The dihedral factor is taken from Geometric Ethics, Chapter 8, and Geometric Law, Chapter 5. The chapter describes it as generated by the correlative and negation symmetries of the four Hohfeldian positions.
  • The 8.9-sigma framing effect and the 100% cross-lingual deontic transfer cited as evidence are quoted as established results, the second from Geometric Communication and Geometric Ethics. This volume reports them and does not measure them.
Prior artA gauge group in the sense of gauge theory in physics, which the chapter cites through Weyl and through Yang and Mills.

Alignment gauge violation tensor instrument

DefinitionA matrix V with one row per type of gauge transformation and one column per output dimension. Entry $V_{ij}$ is the root-mean-square change of the system's output on dimension j when a random transformation of type i is applied to the input. Zero means the output is invariant.
ExampleIf a paraphrase moves the output on one dimension by 0.1 on one scenario and by 0.3 on another, the entry is the square root of (0.01 + 0.09) / 2, which is the square root of 0.05, about 0.22.
VolumeGeometric AI, Volume 11 of the Geometric Series; entry id alignment-gauge-violation-tensor, kind instrument.

It adds that no alignment instrument has been evaluated under the xbse admission filter, and the front matter says that ARIA, the system whose numbers fill the chapter tables, is fictional. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • It needs a set of scenarios, a set of content-preserving transformations of each, and the system’s output on every dimension. A transformation that fails to preserve content produces a false violation, which is why Chapter 15 sends flagged cases to human review.
  • An entry is flagged when it exceeds a threshold that the deployment context sets. The volume gives no universal threshold.
  • The only full tensor printed, 5 transformation types by 9 dimensions on 200 scenarios, is the fictional ARIA’s. The README says no alignment instrument has been evaluated.

alignment, span and curvature of a pairing result

DefinitionThe volume's conjecture that pairing quality is a function of three geometric quantities. Alignment is the cosine of the two flavor vectors, span is how much of the space they jointly cover, and curvature is the symmetric bilinear interaction $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{f}_1, \mathbf{f}_2)$ added to their sum. A single-number summary discards two of the three.
ExampleTwo unit vectors at angle 0 sum to a vector of length 2 in the same direction. Two at a right angle sum to length square root of 2, about 1.41, in a new direction. Their cosines are 1 and 0, and neither number records the resultant or any interaction term.
VolumeGeometric Gastronomy, Volume 12 of the Geometric Series; entry id pairing-alignment-span-curvature, kind result.
StatusA conjecture in the volume's own tagging. The volume presents it as the kitchen form of scalar irrecoverability, which it cites from Volume 4 and does not prove here. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Tagged a conjecture. The volume says the cross-corpus validation is still partial.
  • The interaction term is a modeling axiom. It adds along an axis for synergy, as with salt and umami, subtracts for antagonism, as with sweet and bitter, and is zero in a flat space.
  • Similar summands add nearly colinearly and complementary summands add by the Pythagorean rule. Both statements are for the linear sum without the interaction term.
  • The claim that the three-term model tracks recipe co-occurrence and panel ratings better than cosine alone is stated without printed numbers.

anisotropic concept

DefinitionOf a covariance, having different variances in different directions. Chapter 0. Also anisotrop.
ExampleCovariance diag(0.3, 1.7) has variance 0.3 along the first axis and 1.7 along the second, so it is anisotropic.

Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Of a covariance, having different variances in different directions, which is to say unequal eigenvalues. Two readers at different angles to an anisotropic covariance read different variances, and the flip between two codes exists exactly when the covariance is anisotropic along the directions that separate them.

anti arm instrument

DefinitionIn a flip comparison, a third code built to destroy the consumer's read subspace at the same bits. It is expected to score worst, and a comparison in which it does not is not a flip. Chapter 4. Also anti-arm.
ExamplePut the whole error of 0.4 on the direction the reader reads and the reader sees 0.4; put it on the other direction and the reader sees zero.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id anti-arm, kind instrument.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 4.5.

Assumptions and scope
  • The anti arm is matched on bits with the other two codes, and its purpose is to show that the read subspace is what the comparison is about, since destroying it should be worst.
  • A comparison in which the anti arm is not worst has not shown a flip, whatever the other two arms did.

anti-hub concept

DefinitionA row that is never or almost never retrieved as anyone's nearest neighbour. Chapter 10 names five kinds and shows one is manufactured by the query budget. Chapters 3 and 10.
ExampleWith 1000 queries at k equal to 10 there are 10000 slots, so in a corpus of 100000 rows at least 90 percent are never retrieved.

Book equation 10.3.

Assumptions and scope
  • An anti-hub is a row no query retrieves, and chapter 10 names five kinds, of which one is manufactured by the query budget rather than by the corpus.
  • Anti-hubs are where compressed indexes fail first, since quantization rounds away the fine distinctions by which they are found, while aggregate recall barely moves, which is why recall is reported per stratum with the anti-hub stratum named.

anti-hub recall instrument

DefinitionRecall at k restricted to the rows that are rarely retrieved, the observer's outliers, reported as the minimum over strata so that a mean cannot hide the tail. Chapter 10.
ExampleSeven strata of rarely retrieved rows scored between 0.62 and 0.69, so the minimum, 0.663, failed the bar of 0.90.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id anti-hub-recall, kind instrument.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Recall at k restricted to the rows that are rarely retrieved, the observer’s outliers, reported as the minimum over strata so that a mean cannot hide the tail. It lies in the unit interval and is one exactly when every anti-hub’s true neighbours are returned.
  • Compressed indexes fail on anti-hubs first while aggregate recall barely moves, and the remedy that promotes isolated rows is the remedy that compression damages first, which is why the gate is a build gate and not a report line.

anti-monotonicity concept

DefinitionThe property that support cannot increase when an itemset grows, which licenses Apriori to prune every superset of an infrequent itemset without loss. Chapter 5. Also anti-monoton, pruning license.
ExampleIf bread and butter appear together in 30 baskets, then bread, butter, and jam appear together in at most 30.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id anti-monotonicity, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The property that support cannot increase when an itemset grows, since every transaction containing the larger set contains the smaller. It licenses Apriori to prune every superset of an infrequent itemset without loss, because no frequent itemset can lie above an infrequent one.
  • The license is a statement about the measure and not about the data, and the book’s sidebar carries it to thresholds outside itemsets, where the analogous license is the ceiling on a score that a Youden bound supplies.

Apriori principle result

DefinitionThe statement that every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent, the contrapositive of anti-monotonicity. Chapter 5. Also Apriori, anti-monotonic.
ExampleIf the pair bread and jam is infrequent, every superset such as bread, jam, and milk is skipped without being counted.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id apriori, kind result.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 5.3.

Assumptions and scope
  • Support cannot increase when an itemset grows, so an infrequent itemset has only infrequent supersets and every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent. This holds for any finite collection of transactions.
  • The principle licenses pruning the lattice above an infrequent itemset without counting, and the count of candidates rather than the count of transactions decides whether the run finishes.

Arrow's theorem, geometrized result

DefinitionFor a preference manifold of effective dimension at least 3, no contraction to a one-dimensional social ranking preserves all of topology, orientation and symmetry. These are the volume's readings of independence of irrelevant alternatives, unanimity and non-dictatorship.
ExampleOn a six-dimensional manifold a contraction to a single ranking must drop \(6 - 1 = 5\) dimensions of information, while the three conditions together ask that none be dropped.
VolumeGeometric Politics, Volume 10 of the Geometric Series; entry id geometrized-arrow-theorem, kind result.
StatusA reinterpretation of an established theorem, supported in the chapter by a proof sketch and not a full proof. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The chapter gives a proof sketch. It says the full proof follows Arrow’s original argument reinterpreted geometrically.
  • The impossibility is tied to the one-dimensional output. The volume says cardinal scoring, proportional seat shares and a full-manifold output relax it, with the Gibbard-Satterthwaite constraint on strategic voting still in force.
  • The translation of each axiom into a geometric condition is the volume’s interpretation.

assessment gauge invariance concept

DefinitionAn assessment A, which maps a learner state x and an instrument I to a score, is gauge-invariant when $A(x, I_1)$ and $A(x, I_2)$ differ by no more than measurement noise for every state and every meaning-preserving change of instrument. The volume names five such changes, of examiner, format, language, time and context.
ExampleA student scores 82 on a free-response form and 74 on a multiple-choice form of the same content, and the noise bound is 3 points. The difference of 8 exceeds 3, so for this pair of instruments the assessment is not gauge-invariant.
VolumeGeometric Education, Volume 9 of the Geometric Series; entry id assessment-gauge-invariance, kind concept.
StatusNamed a theorem in the volume. The statement is a criterion that defines a gauge-invariant assessment, and it is the education form of the Bias Invariance Principle of Geometric Reasoning. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • It does not require identical performance on every instrument. It requires the measured understanding to be the same once instrument-specific variance is removed.
  • The volume calls it a necessary condition for assessment validity. Variance tied to the instrument is treated as systematic bias and not as noise.
  • Which changes of instrument preserve meaning is posited. The volume’s argument that format changes the score is that formats project onto different learner dimensions.
  • The effect sizes quoted for the five changes are cited from the literature in general terms. The volume ran no study, and Prediction 16.3.2 on format has not been tested.
Prior artThe Bias Invariance Principle of Geometric Reasoning, which the volume names as its source.

Assessment Gauge Invariance Test Battery (AGITB) instrument

DefinitionFive parallel assessments of the same content, each varying one of examiner, format, language, time and context while holding the others fixed, each with a pass threshold. The composite score is GIS, equal to 1 minus the mean over the five tests of the smaller of 1 and the ratio of the effect size to its threshold.
ExampleIf the five ratios of effect size to threshold are 0.5, 1.0, 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3, their mean is 2.5 divided by 5, which is 0.5, and GIS is 1 minus 0.5, which is 0.5. That is below 0.60, the band the appendix does not recommend for consequential decisions.
VolumeGeometric Education, Volume 9 of the Geometric Series; entry id gauge-invariance-test-battery, kind instrument.
StatusA proposed instrument. The README states that no education-domain instrument has been evaluated by the series' admission filter and that none currently passes its gate. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The thresholds are an effect size below 0.20 for format, language and context, below 0.15 for time, and a kappa of at least 0.80 or an intraclass correlation of at least 0.85 for examiners.
  • The bands are GIS of 0.80 or more as adequate, 0.60 to 0.80 as moderate violation, and below 0.60 as not recommended for consequential decisions.
  • The examiner test is scored by a reliability, where higher is better, and the other four by an effect size, where lower is better. The appendix does not say how the examiner test enters the composite formula.
  • The appendix asks for at least 50 students per test and recommends ethics review. The battery is proposed, and the volume reports no administration of it.
Prior artnone recorded

Asymmetric edge weight (legal) concept

DefinitionThe weight of a directed edge from case $i$ to case $j$ is the quadratic form $\Delta v^T \Sigma^{-1} \Delta v$, plus a penalty $\beta$ for each regime boundary crossed, plus a hierarchical cost. That cost is 0 from a higher court to a lower one, a positive constant $\eta$ at the same level, and infinite from lower to higher.
ExampleIn the volume’s illustration the edge from McDonnell Douglas (Supreme Court) to a district case has quadratic form 5.3125, no boundary crossing and hierarchical cost 0, so its weight is 5.3125 + 0 + 0 = 5.3125. The reverse edge has infinite weight.
VolumeGeometric Law, Volume 5 of the Geometric Series; entry id legal-edge-weight, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic status of 2026-07-14 calls the volume a posited framework with one instrumented corner. That corner is the legal text embedding LeBSE, validated in the xbse admission filter on US case law with labels from the CourtListener citation graph, and the README says this covers structure preservation in legal text embeddings and not the book's broader jurisprudential claims, which remain posited theory at licensed strength. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The weight is asymmetric, so it is a cost function for shortest paths on a directed graph and not a metric. The volume states that only the doctrinal term taken alone is a metric.
  • The formula uses the quadratic form without the square root, although the chapter labels that term the Mahalanobis distance. The worked example adds the squared value to the other two terms.
  • The boundary penalties are to be estimated from the observed cost of crossing jurisdictional, doctrinal, statutory and constitutional boundaries. The volume gives no estimated values.
  • Chapter 15 gives a different operational weight, a cross-validated mix of a citation-type term, an attribute-distance term and an outcome term.
