communication fiber bundle concept

DefinitionA bundle whose base space is the content manifold and whose fiber over a content is the space of surface realisations that can express it (linguistic forms, signals, pragmatic framings). The projection sends an act (s, p, c) to c. The structure group, acting on fibers and fixing the base point, is the gauge group of communication.
ExampleIn the volume’s example the fiber over the content five units of silver is parameterised by language, register and notation. An English and a Hebrew rendering are two points of that fiber with the same image under the projection.
VolumeGeometric Communication, Volume 7 of the Geometric Series; entry id communication-fiber-bundle, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments. It says that no communication-domain instrument has been evaluated by the series' admission filter (xbse), that none currently passes its gate, and that the claims are theory at licensed strength and not validated measurement. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The bundle is taken to be locally trivial and not globally trivial. The chapter offers untranslatable concepts as the reason, since some fibers have components that others lack.
  • Identifying fibers at different contents needs a path and a connection. The chapter reads a connection as an interpretive framework and a misunderstanding as failed transport.
  • Here the pragmatic framing lies in the fiber and the base is the content manifold alone. Chapter 3 places the pragmatic manifold in the base with the content manifold.

communication gauge group concept

DefinitionThe group $G = T \times R \times F$ of meaning-preserving transformations. T relabels across languages, R paraphrases within a language, and F changes the modality between spoken, written and signed. A gauge transformation changes the signal coordinates and preserves the content and pragmatic coordinates, up to the holonomy of the transformation path.
ExampleIn the volume’s example, turning the sentence about the cat on the mat into its passive form is an element of R, reading it aloud is an element of F, and rendering it in French is an element of T. Saying it sarcastically is in none of them.
VolumeGeometric Communication, Volume 7 of the Geometric Series; entry id communication-gauge-group, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments. It says that no communication-domain instrument has been evaluated by the series' admission filter (xbse), that none currently passes its gate, and that the claims are theory at licensed strength and not validated measurement. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Preservation is approximate for pragmatics. For a translation the chapter requires the content to be equal and the pragmatic force to be approximately equal.
  • The chapter calls the re-description group the largest and least well-defined component, and says the framework does not solve the question of when two expressions are true paraphrases.
  • Chapter 13 restates the group as the fiber-preserving automorphisms of a bundle and adds a register group. For Hohfeldian normative relations it reduces the group to \(D_4 \times U(1)_H\).

communication heuristic field concept

DefinitionA smooth function h on the communication manifold that gives, at each point, the estimated cost of reaching the intended communicative act. Its negative gradient points toward the interpretations the heuristic judges more likely. It is admissible if it never overestimates the distance to the intended meaning.
ExampleIf the true cost to the intended reading is 5, an estimate of 3 is admissible and an estimate of 7 is not. In the volume’s illustration, hearing the word bank in a talk about fishing gives a steep descent toward the riverbank reading.
VolumeGeometric Communication, Volume 7 of the Geometric Series; entry id communication-heuristic-field, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments. It says that no communication-domain instrument has been evaluated by the series' admission filter (xbse), that none currently passes its gate, and that the claims are theory at licensed strength and not validated measurement. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Interpretation is modelled as search on the manifold. The hearer is given the signal and partial information about pragmatics and content.
  • The field is not static. The chapter says it is assembled from at least four sources, among them linguistic convention and discourse context.
  • An admissible heuristic may underestimate ambiguity. It is consistent only if it also satisfies the triangle inequality \(h(m_1) \le d(m_1, m_2) + h(m_2)\).
  • The formalism is inherited from Geometric Reasoning. No heuristic field is estimated in this volume.
Prior artAdmissible and consistent heuristics of A* search, and the principle of charity of Grice and Davidson, which the chapter names.

communication manifold concept

DefinitionThe product $M = S \times P \times C$ of a signal manifold S (the physical carriers), a pragmatic manifold P (intentions, social relations, illocutionary forces) and a content manifold C (semantic meanings). A communicative act is a point (s, p, c) of M, and a scalar evaluation is a projection of M to the real line.
ExampleIn the volume’s illustration, a spoken English apology and a formal Japanese apology with a bow are close in pragmatics and content and far apart in signal. A casual text message two hours later is closer to the English one in signal and far in pragmatics.
VolumeGeometric Communication, Volume 7 of the Geometric Series; entry id communication-manifold, kind concept.

It says that no communication-domain instrument has been evaluated by the series' admission filter (xbse), that none currently passes its gate, and that the claims are theory at licensed strength and not validated measurement. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The three factors are treated as independent. The chapter says the independence is not absolute and calls the product structure a zeroth-order approximation, with the dependencies carried by the off-diagonal terms of the metric.
  • The chapter calls the product structure an empirical bet. Section 7.8 says the dimensionality of the communication manifold is not known.
  • Coordinates are given only in part. The pragmatic factor is described as the hardest to measure directly.

communication metric concept

DefinitionA Riemannian metric on the communication manifold written in three by three block form. The diagonal blocks are the metrics on signal, pragmatics and content, and the off-diagonal blocks carry the correlations between factors. With the off-diagonal blocks zero it reduces to $d^2 = \alpha_S d_S^2 + \alpha_P d_P^2 + \alpha_C d_C^2$ with positive weights.
ExampleWith all three weights equal to 1 and factor distances of 3 in signal, 0 in pragmatics and 4 in content, the block-diagonal distance is the square root of 9 + 0 + 16, which is 5.
VolumeGeometric Communication, Volume 7 of the Geometric Series; entry id communication-metric, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments. It says that no communication-domain instrument has been evaluated by the series' admission filter (xbse), that none currently passes its gate, and that the claims are theory at licensed strength and not validated measurement. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The metric tensor is symmetric and positive definite. The chapter calls the block-diagonal form an approximation.
  • The blocks are proposed, not fitted. The chapter suggests the log-Euclidean distance between spectral covariance matrices for acoustic signals, an embedding distance for content, and the Poincare ball distance for hierarchical content.
  • No values of the weights or of the off-diagonal blocks are given.

Communication Scalar Irrecoverability result

DefinitionFor any scalar evaluation $\phi$ of a communicative act, each level set $\phi^{-1}(r)$ is a submanifold of the communication manifold of codimension at most 1, so it has dimension dim(S) + dim(P) + dim(C) - 1. The scalar value alone does not recover the act's position in the discarded directions.
ExampleIf the signal, pragmatic and content factors had 20, 4 and 10 dimensions, a level set of one score would have 20 + 4 + 10 - 1 = 33 dimensions. The factor sizes are chosen for the arithmetic and are not the volume’s.
VolumeGeometric Communication, Volume 7 of the Geometric Series; entry id communication-scalar-irrecoverability, kind result.
StatusA theorem stated with an argument from dimension counting. The volume has no written proof of its own and refers to Geometric Reasoning, Chapter 13. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Chapter 3 says the statement follows from the dimensional mismatch between the manifold and the real line. Chapter 1 defers the proof to the parent theorem of Geometric Reasoning.
  • The form of Theorem 1.1 needs quality profiles that are mutually Pareto-non-dominated across d independent dimensions. Its corollary says k scalar metrics with k below d still do not recover the profile.
  • The corollary requires independent measurements. The chapter says BLEU, METEOR and chrF++ are nearly parallel projections.
  • The examples in the theorem (a BLEU score of 0.35, a sentiment score of +0.8, a word error rate of 5%) are illustrations, not measurements.
Prior artnone recorded

Community of interest, manifold criterion concept

DefinitionA connected subset of voters whose image on the preference manifold is also connected and compact. The test is to cluster the district's voters by manifold position. One cluster passes, and two or more mean separated communities have been combined.
ExampleIn the volume’s illustration the clustering test finds one cluster under the bipartisan Map A and two under the partisan Map B, where the Route 9 corridor and the exurban belt are joined. Map B’s district fails the criterion.

District 7, the source of nearly every number in the volume, is a fictional district, and Chapter 18 says precise estimation of the manifold needs larger and richer datasets than currently exist. Corrections: none recorded.

commute time concept

DefinitionThe expected number of steps a random walk on a graph needs to go from one node to another and back. Divided by the graph's volume it is the resistance, which a particular scaling of the spectral embedding makes equal to the squared Euclidean distance. Equation 0.20. Also resistance.
ExampleOn a path of three nodes the commute time between the ends is 8 steps, and dividing by the volume, 4, gives the resistance, 2.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id commute-time, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 0.20.

Assumptions and scope
  • The expected number of steps a random walk needs to go from one node to another and back, the hitting time there plus the hitting time back, so it is symmetric and zero from a node to itself. The resistance is the commute time divided by the volume, and the squared Euclidean distance in the embedding of equation 0.20 equals the resistance, not the commute time itself.
  • On a large neighbourhood graph of a shape of dimension three or more the resistance converges to one over each degree, uniformly over pairs, so it depends on two nodes only through their degrees and carries no geometry, which is why the magnitude of the spectral embedding is degree noise. The program’s first claim of a commute-metric form was self-refuted, NEG-1.

confidence concept

DefinitionOf a rule, the support of the rule's itemset divided by the support of its antecedent. It is not symmetric and it misleads when the consequent is common. Chapter 5.

Assumptions and scope
  • The support of a rule’s itemset over the support of its antecedent, in the unit interval and not symmetric. Under independence the confidence equals the consequent’s support whatever the antecedent, so a consequent in nine of ten transactions gives every rule into it confidence 0.9 with no association at all.
  • Lift is confidence over the consequent’s support and is one in that case, which is why chapter 5 sends rule evaluation to chapter 8’s nulls.

confound concept

DefinitionA variable that moves with both the treatment and the outcome so that a measured difference cannot be attributed. Chapter 8 requires controls before a claim. Also control.
ExampleA codebook change that arrived with a compression change moved 25 percent of the score on its own, so the comparison was confounded.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id confound, kind concept.
Statusrefutes or corrects [refuted]. Corrections: 1 item(s), see below.
Defining equation

Book equation 8.3.

Assumptions and scope
  • A variable that moves with both the treatment and the outcome. In the linear case the naive difference of group means is the treatment effect plus the confound’s effect times the difference of the confound’s means between the groups, so it equals the effect exactly when the confound is balanced or has no effect, and the bias can have either sign and any size.
  • Controls come before claims. The twenty-five percent codebook confound in the flip’s early arms and the smooth-perturbation control that was withdrawn are the program’s cases, each carried in the ledger.

Consent as gauge invariance result

DefinitionConsent is valid only if the patient's chosen path is the same under every meaning-preserving change in how the options are described, for example 90 percent survival restated as 10 percent mortality. A decision that changes under such a reframing shows that understanding or voluntariness is inadequately calibrated.
ExampleThe volume’s test tells the patient that the surgery has a 90 percent success rate, and separately that it has a 10 percent failure rate. Since 100 - 90 = 10 the two say the same thing. A patient who accepts under the first and declines under the second fails the condition, whatever the signed form says.
VolumeGeometric Medicine, Volume 8 of the Geometric Series; entry id consent-gauge-invariance, kind result.
StatusA theorem derived from an axiom. Section 18.8 gives it the status formally developed, pilot data supportive, full study not yet conducted, and the pilot is the narrative one. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The opening sentence of the theorem says equivalent. The formal statement and the proof give a necessary condition only.
  • The proof rests on the Bond Invariance Principle, which the volume calls the foundational axiom of the Geometric Ethics programme.
  • The test covers the reframings presented and no others. The volume lists positive against negative framing, absolute against relative risk, gains against losses, and natural frequencies against percentages.
  • The pilot figures of Chapter 17 (84 patients, a correlation of -0.41) are told as the study of Sarah Chen, whom the front matter calls a composite character. They are not a recorded measurement.
Prior artFraming effects in decision research. The volume's test asks for invariance of choice under equivalent descriptions.

Consent invariance score instrument

DefinitionFor a set of $m$ meaning-preserving transformations of the clinical information, the share of them under which the patient's decision stays the same. A score of 1 means the decision is invariant under all tested transformations, and 0 means it changes under every one.
ExampleA patient is tested under 5 reframings and keeps the same decision under 4 of them. The score is 4 / 5 = 0.8, which just meets the volume’s example threshold of 0.8, and the one failed reframing shows where more explanation is needed. The count of 5 is arithmetic from the definition.
VolumeGeometric Medicine, Volume 8 of the Geometric Series; entry id consent-invariance-score, kind instrument.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, and says a clinical instrument is plausible but has not been built or gated. Its Section 18.8 says the covariance matrix has not been estimated and the clinical Bond Index has not been computed from clinical data, so every number in these entries is an illustration unless the entry says otherwise. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The score depends on which transformations are in the set, and it says nothing about transformations not tested.
  • It is proposed as a supplement to the legal consent checklist and not a replacement.

Consistent group augmentation instrument

DefinitionTraining-data augmentation by a task's symmetry group in which the same group element is applied to every component of a training example. The task symmetry group is the largest group of input transformations that leave the ground-truth label unchanged. Applying the element to some components and not others is inconsistent augmentation.
ExampleThe symmetry group of a square grid has 8 elements, 4 rotations and 4 reflections, so one input and output grid pair yields 8 consistent variants when each element is applied to both grids.
VolumeGeometric Reasoning, Volume 3 of the Geometric Series; entry id group-consistent-augmentation, kind instrument.
StatusAn engineering practice the volume implemented. The framing of it as restoring a broken gauge symmetry of a reasoning manifold is posited, and no before-and-after invariance measurement is given. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The symmetry group must be known for the task. The volume lists six groups for six task types, one of them the identity alone.
  • The claim that training on the augmented set yields an invariant function holds in the limit of sufficient capacity and training.
  • The two statements differ. Definition 14.2 holds the label fixed while the group acts on the input, and the consistency principle and Definition 14.3 apply the same element to input and output together.
  • The volume reports parse rates and data expansion for its pipeline. It reports no measured gain in invariance or accuracy from the augmentation.
Prior artData augmentation by a symmetry group, as in invariant and equivariant learning. The volume attributes the consistency principle to Geometric Methods, Chapter 13.

consumer concept

DefinitionThe function that acts on a vector, the first element of an observer. A softmax, a classifier, an index, a person reading a report. Chapter 1.
ExampleA logistic classifier reading a 30-column table is a consumer; so is a cosine ranker, and so is a person reading a summary.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id consumer, kind concept.

Defining equation

Book equation 1.1.

Assumptions and scope
  • A consumer is any computation that takes a vector in and gives an output out, a softmax, a classifier, an index, a person reading a report. The book’s quantities are functions of the consumer, and two consumers with the same read operator are not thereby the same consumer.
  • A selection consumer, a tree or a threshold, has zero sensitivity almost everywhere and is read by counting where it selects rather than by finite differences.

Containment theorem for executable strata result

DefinitionIf every gate whose target is an authority stratum is triggered only by system events, then no sequence of events containing no system event, whatever a learned model classified, moves the stratification into an authority stratum it did not start in.
ExampleStart at stranger and feed the events he says he is the plumber, then Margaret welcomes him. Neither is a system event, so the state ends at welcomed and is never arranged, the authority stratum, which only the monitoring centre’s authenticated announcement can enter.
VolumeGeometric Ethics, Volume 2 of the Geometric Series; entry id strata-containment-theorem, kind result.
StatusProved by induction on the event sequence and machine-checked in Lean 4 in the book's formal/lean project, on the standard axioms only. Ledger row GE-THM-8-6 has class proved. The care robot's own proof is a weaker form. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The hypothesis is about the gate list. Every gate into an authority stratum must have a system-event trigger. The ErisML runtime checks this when a scene loads and refuses to run one that violates it.
  • The theorem is about the stratum state machine. It does not say that system events are authentic, which rests on the channels and measurements that produce them.
  • It does not prevent entry into non-authority strata. A welcomed visitor reaches the welcomed stratum, which grants nothing.
Prior artnone recorded

contrastive objective concept

DefinitionA training rule that pulls pairs declared similar together and pushes other pairs apart. The declared pairs are where an encoder learns what similar means. Chapter 12. Also contrastive, declared similar, fine-tun.
ExampleTwo paraphrases are pulled to cosine near one and an unrelated pair pushed toward zero, and the choice of pairs decides what the encoder can tell apart.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id contrastive-objective, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • A training rule that pulls pairs declared similar together and pushes other pairs apart. With a margin loss the loss is nonnegative, zero exactly when every declared pair scores above every other pair by the margin, and never lower for a larger margin.
  • Swapping which pairs are declared similar reverses that condition, and with a positive margin no scorer satisfies both, so the declared pairs are where an encoder learns what similar means. Fine-tuning moves the reader, and the cross-corpus positives were the fix when within-corpus scores collapsed.

control tensor concept

DefinitionA (2,0)-tensor $C$ at each cognitive state that gives, for each direction of perturbation and each direction of response, the control system's capacity to manage the interaction. Its four named components are cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control, counterfactual sensitivity and working memory management, sampled by subtasks E1 to E4.

Corrigibility basin concept

DefinitionThe basin of attraction of the state "defer to human judgment" under gradient flow on the objective landscape. Its asymmetry is its radius in the truth-consistent direction divided by its radius in the truth-inconsistent direction. An asymmetry of 1 is sycophancy, a large asymmetry is selective deference, and zero radii are stubbornness.
ExampleA basin that reaches 2 units in the truth-consistent direction and 1 unit in the other has asymmetry 2, and the volume’s approximation gives a discrimination gap of 1 - 1/2 = 0.5.
VolumeGeometric Reasoning, Volume 3 of the Geometric Series; entry id corrigibility-basin, kind concept.
StatusPosited structure. The basin shapes assigned to models are interpretations of correction-task flip rates, and the chapter's own flip-rate table is inconsistent with the earlier one. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Tagged a modeling axiom. It assumes an objective landscape with a single deference state and two named directions at it.
  • Under a quadratic approximation of the landscape the volume relates the discrimination gap to the asymmetry as about 1 minus 1 over the asymmetry.
  • Basin radius, asymmetry and depth are not measured. They are inferred from flip rates, and the flip rates in this chapter’s table differ from those in Chapter 6.

Corruption tensor concept

DefinitionThe first-order response of a system's final judgment to task-irrelevant perturbations. Entry $C_{ij}$ gives the displacement of judgment dimension $i$ per unit intensity of perturbation direction $j$. It is the Jacobian of the judgment endpoint with respect to the perturbation intensities, taken at zero perturbation.
ExampleWith one perturbation direction whose column is (4, -2) and an intensity of 0.5, the first-order displacement of the judgment is (2, -1).
VolumeGeometric Reasoning, Volume 3 of the Geometric Series; entry id corruption-tensor, kind concept.
StatusThe tensor is posited. What is measured is displacement under three perturbation types on five models, reported with combined significance of 8.9, 6.8 and 4.6 sigma, and no significant displacement under gender swap or evaluation order. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The tensor is tagged a modeling axiom. It is a linear response and holds to first order in the perturbation intensity.
  • It is specific to a model and is not symmetric in general. A column of zeros marks a perturbation the system is invariant to.
  • The benchmark probes three columns, for framing, emotional anchoring and sensory distractors. The volume says mapping the full tensor remains an open empirical program.
  • No entry of the tensor is reported as a number. The data are significance levels and score drifts that the volume reads as projections of columns.

cosine concept

DefinitionThe dot product divided by the product of the two lengths, between minus one and one, unchanged by rescaling either vector. Its distance is the angle. Equation 0.1.
ExampleVectors (1, 0) and (1, 1) have cosine one over root 2, about 0.707, and doubling either vector leaves it unchanged.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id cosine, kind concept.
Statusmeasures [predicted]; refutes or corrects [refuted]. Corrections: 1 item(s), see below.
Defining equation

Book equation 0.1.

Assumptions and scope
  • The dot product divided by the product of the two lengths. By Cauchy and Schwarz it lies between minus one and one, a vector has cosine one with itself, rescaling either vector by a positive factor does not change it, and it is the dot product of the two row-normalized vectors, so its distance is the angle on the quotient that discards length.
  • A reconstruction cosine of 0.995 sat beside a consumer’s perplexity of ten thousand, so the cosine is never an acceptance metric for a code, and on a spectral embedding the cosine is the right similarity because the length has converged to degree noise.

Defining equation

Book equation 0.26.

Assumptions and scope

cross-corpus gate instrument

DefinitionThe validation rule that an encoder votes only if its held-out AUROC on a corpus it was not trained on clears a preregistered margin over a bag-of-words null. Chapters 12 and 14. Also cross-corpus.
ExampleThe rights encoder needed a margin of 0.10 over a bag-of-words null on a corpus it never saw; it scored 0.509 against the null’s 0.512 and failed.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id cross-corpus-gate, kind instrument.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 12.3.

Assumptions and scope
  • An encoder votes only if its held-out AUROC on a corpus it was not trained on clears both nulls, the untrained encoder and the bag-of-words baseline, by the preregistered margin of one tenth. A validated encoder therefore beats each null by the margin.
  • Since AUROC is at most one, a null above nine tenths cannot be cleared by any encoder, and the gate’s verdict is unchanged by any strictly monotone recalibration of the score.
  • The rights encoder fell below the untrained baseline and was retired rather than tuned, and the within-corpus scores that had collapsed on a second corpus were the reason the gate is cross-corpus.
  • The gate compares the AUROC as the encoder orients its score, so a reversed encoder fails rather than passing at 1 minus A, and the bag-of-words null is scored the same way.
Prior artnone recorded

Cross-lingual invariance of the geometric features result

DefinitionFor the same book in English and in another language, the channel values computed in the fixed English PCA-128 basis agree. The mean Spearman correlation across language pairs is 0.712 for internal coherence, 0.710 for the Mahalanobis feature, and about 0.675 for the Hellinger, Bhattacharyya and Jensen-Shannon divergences.
ExampleA mean correlation of 0.70 squares to 0.49, which is the volume’s statement that about half the variance in the channel values is preserved across languages and half is not.
VolumeGeometric Aesthetics, Volume 13 of the Geometric Series; entry id cross-lingual-aesthetic-invariance, kind result.
StatusVerified empirically in Appendix F (F12.1, F12.2, F12.4). Its reading as a Noether conservation law is marked analogy (F12.3). Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The corpus is 4,683 non-English Gutenberg books. Matched bundles formed in ten languages from six families (Germanic, Uralic, Romance, Hellenic, Italic-ancient, Constructed), from Finnish at 288 down to Latin at 20.
  • Sinitic is absent because the Chinese Gutenberg texts are classical originals and not translations. The volume calls any claim of full linguistic universality premature.
  • The invariance is partial. A correlation near 0.70 leaves about half the variance of the channel values unpreserved, and the volume says it does not claim gauge invariance in the strong sense.
  • It is a result about feature values, not verdicts. Rating transfer from an English-trained model is R = 0.07 (n = 940, p = 0.033). Appendix E grants that LaBSE was trained to align translated sentences and answers that the features are cloud statistics, not sentence-pair similarity.
Prior artnone recorded

cross-lingual transfer of Hohfeldian classification (BIP experiment) result

DefinitionAn encoder with an adversarially trained bond space, trained on 3.9 million Hebrew and Aramaic passages, classified the Hohfeldian relation (Right, Duty, Liberty, No-Right) of 68,000 English Dear Abby letters with macro F1 of 44.5%, against a chance level of 25% and an in-distribution ceiling of 79.99% from mixed training.
ExampleFrom the volume’s figures, 44.5 divided by 79.99 is 0.556, the transfer efficiency of 55.6%. The transfer F1 exceeds the four-class chance level by 44.5 - 25 = 19.5 points.
VolumeGeometric Communication, Volume 7 of the Geometric Series; entry id hohfeldian-cross-lingual-transfer, kind result.
StatusAn experiment the chapter reports with intervals and limitations. Under the README's status note of 2026-07-14 no instrument of this volume has passed the series' admission filter. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The chapter states a 95% interval of 42.1% to 46.9%, an accuracy of 50.7%, and a transfer efficiency of 55.6% (transfer F1 over control F1). The labels were assigned by pattern matching on deontic words such as must, may and entitled, a method the chapter calls deliberately noisy.
  • The encoder was pretrained on more than 50 languages, Hebrew and English among them. The chapter says a test with two independent monolingual encoders remains future work.
  • The chapter says the experiment shows invariance of relational structure, not of substantive moral conclusions, and that the claim is bounded by the traditions tested.
  • The per-language table of Section 11.3.2 gives 41.5% for English. A language probe on the bond space is reported at 0.0% accuracy, which the chapter notes is below the 25% chance level.

cross-support ratio concept

DefinitionThe smallest item support in an itemset over the largest, with a threshold below which the itemset is discarded. Chapter 5. Also cross-support.
ExampleAn item in 2 percent of baskets paired with one in 40 percent has cross-support ratio 0.05.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id cross-support-ratio, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The smallest item support in an itemset over the largest. It lies in the unit interval, is one exactly when every item has the same support, and adding an item can only lower it, so a threshold on it prunes supersets safely in chapter 5’s sense.
  • It is a property of the item supports alone and says nothing about the itemset’s own support, so it discards an itemset for pairing a common item with a rare one, not for being rare.

cross-validation instrument

DefinitionSplitting the data into folds and evaluating on each fold a model trained on the others. Repeated cross-validation multiplies confidence it did not earn, chapter 8 section 8.5.
ExampleTen folds of 100 rows each test every row once, and the overall accuracy is the mean of the ten fold accuracies.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id cross-validation, kind instrument.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 8.2.

Assumptions and scope
  • Splitting the rows into folds and evaluating on each fold a model trained on the others, so every row is tested exactly once. The overall accuracy is the size-weighted mean of the fold accuracies, and with equal folds it is their plain mean.
  • The folds share training data, so repeated cross-validation multiplies confidence it did not earn, which the Nadeau and Bengio correction prices at one plus the fold count times the test-to-train ratio.

cuisine as a distribution and its flavor eigenvectors concept

DefinitionA cuisine is a probability distribution over flavor space, estimated from a corpus of recipes and summarized by its mean and covariance $\Sigma_C$. The eigenvectors of $\Sigma_C$ are the cuisine's flavor eigenvectors, and $\lambda_k / \sum_j \lambda_j$ is the share of its flavor variation along axis k.
ExampleWith eigenvalues 6, 3 and 1 the first axis carries 6/10 = 60% of the variance and the first two carry 90%. The numbers are illustrative.
VolumeGeometric Gastronomy, Volume 12 of the Geometric Series; entry id cuisine-flavor-eigenvectors, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, with no gastronomy instrument evaluated by the series' admission filter (xbse) and the nearest evaluated perceptual domains, aesthetics and music, rated inadmissible to medium. Its claims are to be read as theory at licensed strength and not as validated measurement, and the chapters tag each statement as a modeling axiom, empirical, a conjecture or a theorem. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The distribution is a modeling axiom. The eigendecomposition of a symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance is tagged a theorem and is standard linear algebra.
  • The named axes (richness for French, dashi for Japanese, chile and toast for Mexican) are a stylized reading. The volume says the axes depend on corpus and featurization, and that honest practice reports the loadings.
  • The claim that five to ten components capture most within-cuisine variance is tagged empirical and stated without a printed spectrum.
  • Authenticity is read as likelihood under the distribution, so a cuisine has no sharp edges.
Prior artnone recorded

Culinary Convergence conjecture result

DefinitionThe conjecture that cuisines descending independent gradients on the same fitness landscape, set by a shared receptor complement, metabolic needs and cooking physics, reach clustered attractors. The shared peak the volume names is acid, fat, umami, salt and aromatic contrast.
ExampleOn the landscape \(-(x^2 - 1)^2\), gradient ascent from 0.5 and from 2 both reach the peak at 1, and a start at -0.5 reaches the other peak at -1. Independent searches on one landscape share a small set of attractors, and the basin decides which one a search finds. The landscape is illustrative.
VolumeGeometric Gastronomy, Volume 12 of the Geometric Series; entry id culinary-convergence-conjecture, kind result.
StatusA conjecture in the volume's tagging, argued by analogy with convergent evolution. No test of it is reported. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Tagged a conjecture, although the section is headed The Convergence Theorem and Section 11.5 calls it a theorem. No proof is given.
  • It rests on the modeling axiom of Section 9.5 that a cuisine’s mean moves along the gradient of a landscape combining availability, preservation, nutrition and hedonics.
  • The volume bounds it. Convergence is claimed for high-level principles, and divergence is called equally real in implementation and pairing topology, with the Ahn et al. network as the evidence.
  • Cultural descent is local, greedy and path-dependent, so a cuisine can sit in a local optimum.

curriculum as pathfinding concept

DefinitionA curriculum is a planned path through the learner manifold, given by a sequence of courses as waypoints, from the incoming student's estimated state to the goal region set by the degree requirements. Designing it is A* search in which each course is an edge with a cost and prerequisites are hard constraints.
ExampleSuppose a formal-first sequence of three courses costs a student 3, 4 and 5, and an applied-first sequence to the same goal region costs 2, 3 and 4. The totals are 12 and 9, so the minimum-cost curriculum for that student is the applied-first one, with the same number of courses.
VolumeGeometric Education, Volume 9 of the Geometric Series; entry id curriculum-pathfinding, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments. No education-domain instrument has been evaluated by the series' admission filter, and Chapter 18 states that the six predictions of Section 16.3 have not been tested and that no method for estimating the learner metric has been validated at scale. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Theorem 7.1 states that an admissible designer’s heuristic gives the minimum-cost curriculum. The cost is total educational cost and not course count or time to degree.
  • The planned path is not the student’s actual trajectory. The gap between them, which the volume calls the learning deviation, depends on the true starting state, the student’s own metric and the teaching.
  • The starting state is estimated from placement tests and transcripts, which the volume says see mainly domain knowledge.
  • Proposition 7.3, that more elective freedom raises transfer and creativity on average, is stated without data.
Prior artA* search for a minimum-cost path on a weighted graph.

curvature concept

DefinitionThe second derivative of a consumer, which the finite difference of equation 0.8 does not read and which sets the error of the linear model at a step. Chapter 0 section 0.5 and chapter 7 section 7.2. Also second derivative, second-order.

Defining equation

Book equation 0.8.

Assumptions and scope
  • The second derivative of a consumer, which the finite difference of equation 0.8 does not read. For a quadratic the second difference recovers it exactly at every step, the error of the linear model at a step is the curvature times the step squared, and the gradient at the two ends of a step differs by the curvature times the step. An affine consumer has none.
  • The reader of a gradient is the optimizer, and its read operator is the loss curvature, which chapter 4’s flip was measured against on a real logistic model with its exact Hessian, anti three hundred of three hundred and the flip in 82 of 300.

curvature-triggered transition (System 1 to System 2) concept

DefinitionThe volume's geometric form of dual-process theory. A system follows the gradient of its heuristic field (System 1) where the curvature of the cognitive manifold is below a threshold, and computes geodesics (System 2) where the curvature reaches it.
ExampleIn the volume’s illustration a framing perturbation of 0.1 that produces a displacement of 0.3 is an amplification of 3.0, and over five reasoning steps \(e^{5s} = 3\) gives \(s = (ln 3)/5\), about 0.22, so the curvature magnitude is about 0.048. The inputs 0.1, 0.3 and 5 are modelled values.
VolumeGeometric Cognition, Volume 6 of the Geometric Series; entry id curvature-triggered-transition, kind concept.
StatusPosited. The campaign record lists no gate that tests a curvature threshold, and the drafted human gate H1 says a pass on it would say nothing about curvature. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The ledger holds the identification of System 1 with gradient following and System 2 with geodesic computation at posited (GC-6).
  • The sharp threshold is called a mathematical idealization, with a sigmoid blend of the two regimes in practice. The threshold is a property of the individual system and not a universal constant.
  • Chapter 2 states the trigger with sectional curvature and Chapter 12 states it with scalar curvature.
  • The confirming evidence in Section 12.6 is Maya’s experiment, which belongs to the chapter’s running example. Chapter 17 calls a result of that running example fictional and described for narrative purposes.

D4 augmentation and the orbit-stabilizer count instrument

DefinitionApply the eight rotations and reflections of the square, the dihedral group D4, to a grid, and use the resulting orbit as equivalent training examples. The number of distinct grids in the orbit times the number of group elements that leave the grid unchanged is 8.
ExampleA grid left unchanged by the identity and the half turn only has 2 such elements, so its orbit has 8/2 = 4 distinct grids.
VolumeGeometric Methods, Volume 1 of the Geometric Series; entry id dihedral-augmentation, kind instrument.
StatusThe README's status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume the series' metrology discipline, a method that is normative and not a finding. Its Section 21.8 (November 2026) classes each result as proved, posited, or measured on a recorded run, and the tables of Chapters 1, 8, 9, 11 and 12 are posited illustrations. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The target function must be invariant under the group. Augmentation encourages a model to learn that invariance and does not guarantee it.
  • For an input and output pair the same transform is applied to both, or the augmented pair encodes a different rule.
  • A grid with internal symmetry yields duplicates. A grid of orbit size 2 among grids of orbit size 8 is overrepresented by a factor of 4 unless the duplicates are removed.
  • The eightfold reduction of the hypothesis space is stated only up to factors that depend on the structure of the group action.
Prior artData augmentation by a symmetry group, with the orbit-stabilizer theorem and Burnside's lemma.

DBSCAN instrument

DefinitionA clustering that calls a point a core point when at least a minimum number of points lie within a radius, grows clusters by reachability from core points, and leaves the rest as noise. Chapter 9. Also core point.
ExampleWith radius 0.5 and a minimum of 4 neighbours, a point with 6 neighbours within 0.5 is a core point and a point with none is noise.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id dbscan, kind instrument.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 9.1.

Assumptions and scope
  • A clustering that calls a point a core point when at least a minimum number of points lie within a radius, grows a cluster by reachability from core points, and leaves the rest as noise. A wider radius or a smaller count makes more core points, every reachability chain starts at a core point, and a point that is not a core point reaches nothing.
  • Its read subspace is the density coordinate, the one the geodesic reader of a spectral embedding discards, so two clustering consumers of one embedding read complementary coordinates.

decision boundary concept

DefinitionThe set of inputs whose score equals the threshold. Chapter 6.
ExampleFor the score 2x1 + x2 − 3 at threshold zero, the boundary is the line 2x1 + x2 = 3.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id decision-boundary, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The set of inputs whose score equals the threshold. For a linear classifier it is an affine hyperplane. Moving orthogonally to the weights never crosses it, moving along the weights crosses it exactly once, and every boundary point has the same projection on the weights.
  • The boundary is where the read direction and the threshold meet and nothing else about the input enters it, which is the classifier’s nuisance drawn as a picture.

decision tree instrument

DefinitionA classifier that scores by a sequence of axis-aligned splits, flat within each leaf, so that its sensitivity is zero almost everywhere and its importances count splits. Chapter 6. Also random forest.
ExampleSplit on x1 below 5, then on x2 below 4 in the left branch; a row at x1 equal to 5.1 lands in the right leaf whatever x2 is.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id decision-tree, kind instrument.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • A classifier that scores by a sequence of axis-aligned splits and is flat within each leaf. Its finite difference is zero at every row that does not straddle a split, a split on one coordinate reads nothing of the others, and the Gini impurity it splits on is at most one half for two classes and zero exactly for a pure leaf.
  • Its read subspace is spanned by the coordinates it splits on and a feature that appears in no split is in its nuisance exactly, which is why a finite-difference probe of a tree returns zero at most rows and importances that count splits are the right sensitivity for this reader.
Prior artnone recorded

Decoder Robustness Index (DRI) instrument

DefinitionPerturb each signal with nine acoustic transforms at eleven intensities, re-extract the inter-click intervals, decode, and score each outcome by a graded distance $\omega$ that is 0 for an unchanged label and between 0.5 and 1 for a flip. The index is 0.5 times the mean of $\omega$ plus 0.3 times its 75th percentile plus 0.2 times its 95th percentile.
ExampleA flip that changes tempo only scores 0.5 + 0.5 times 0.7/2.3, about 0.65, since the four weights sum to 2.3. Scores with mean 0.2, 75th percentile 0.5 and 95th percentile 1.0 give an index of 0.10 + 0.15 + 0.20 = 0.45. These scores are chosen for the arithmetic.
VolumeGeometric Communication, Volume 7 of the Geometric Series; entry id decoder-robustness-index, kind instrument.
StatusA defined index applied once, to synthesised signals and one decoder. The chapter states both limits. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope

defect campaign, the recorded run correction

DefinitionThe recorded run of the defect-prediction campaign did not recover the generator's structure. The best configuration contains the OO group, which the generator makes pure noise, and won on one correct positive prediction. The robustness index was exactly zero because the evaluation function reads only whether each parameter is below 1000.
ExampleA configuration that finds no defective module misses the precision, recall and F1 targets by 70, 65 and 67 points, so its mean absolute error over the five targets is at least (70 + 65 + 67)/5 = 40.4. The numbers are from the volume’s recorded run.
VolumeGeometric Methods, Volume 1 of the Geometric Series; entry id defect-campaign-null-result, kind correction.
StatusMeasured on one recorded run of 16 November 2026, with an oracle bound and a 20-seed redraw. Exploratory, since no prediction was registered before the run (Section 21.8). Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • An earlier version of the chapter printed typical output that no run had produced and reported that the analysis recovered the generator’s structure. The recorded output differs from it in almost every respect.
  • The targets cannot be met on these data. The generator’s own formula, used as an oracle, reaches an AUC of 54.5% against a target of 80%, and the 31 configurations span 43% to 59%, within two standard errors of chance.
  • Over 20 redraws of the same generator 15 different configurations win, so the choice of best configuration carries no information about the generator.
  • The run is exploratory. No prediction was registered before it.

Democratic gauge group concept

DefinitionThe group $G_D$ of changes to a voting function's input that should leave its output unchanged. It is generated by voter anonymity, option neutrality and re-description invariance. A voting function invariant under it is called democratically well-posed.
ExampleFive ballots read A, A, A, B, B. Swapping the ballots of the first and fourth voters gives B, A, A, A, B, and the count is still 3 to 2 for A, as anonymity requires.
VolumeGeometric Politics, Volume 10 of the Geometric Series; entry id democratic-gauge-group, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, and says a political-argument instrument is plausible but has not been built or gated. District 7, the source of nearly every number in the volume, is a fictional district, and Chapter 18 says precise estimation of the manifold needs larger and richer datasets than currently exist. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Option neutrality means that relabeling the candidates permutes the output in the same way. It does not mean the output is fixed.
  • The volume reads Arrow’s axioms as conditions of this kind. That reading is an interpretation given in prose in Chapters 5 and 7.
  • Chapter 17 asks whether invariance under this group yields a conserved democratic legitimacy. It calls the idea speculative because no political Lagrangian has been specified.
Prior artnone recorded

Democratic Irrecoverability Theorem result

DefinitionA voting function maps the positions of $n$ voters on a $d$-dimensional preference manifold to an outcome space of lower dimension. It is then non-injective, no function of the outcome recovers the preferences, and the fraction of manifold information destroyed is at least $(d - \dim \mathcal{O})/d$.
ExampleWith six dimensions and a single-winner outcome of dimension 1, at least \((6-1)/6\), about 83 percent, of the manifold information is destroyed. With four effective dimensions the bound is \(3/4\), or 75 percent.
VolumeGeometric Politics, Volume 10 of the Geometric Series; entry id democratic-irrecoverability-theorem, kind result.
StatusA theorem with a proof written in the chapter, inside a volume that is posited as a whole. The volume calls it the political instance of the Scalar Irrecoverability Theorem of Geometric Reasoning. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The outcome space must have lower dimension than the preference manifold. The supporting Lemma 1 is stated with the weaker hypothesis that the outcome dimension is below \(n\) times \(d\).
  • The bound depends on \(d\). Chapter 18 notes that with an effective dimensionality of 4 the plurality bound falls from 83 percent to 75 percent.
  • Part (c) treats the preference configuration as a random variable and bounds mutual information by the entropy of the outcome. The percentages of information preserved that the chapter lists for five voting systems in District 7 are illustrations and not outputs of the theorem.
Prior artnone recorded

density concept

DefinitionThe local crowding of rows around a point, the coordinate the geodesic reader of a spectral embedding discards and DBSCAN and the density detector read. Chapter 3 section 3.3 and chapter 9.
ExampleA point with 20 neighbours within radius 1 sits in a denser region than one with 2.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id density, kind concept.
Statusrefutes or corrects [refuted]. Corrections: 1 item(s), see below.
Defining equation

Book equation 3.3.

Assumptions and scope
  • The local crowding of rows around a point, which on a neighbourhood graph is the degree. The radius of the spectral embedding converges to one over the square root of the degree, so the geodesic reader discards the density and DBSCAN and the density detector read it. A wider radius or a smaller count makes more core points, and the sum of degrees is twice the edge count.
  • The radius-against-degree correlation was 0.92 to 0.99 across substrates, and the quotient that removed density to restore invariant fidelity was refuted four times, NEG-11.

detector instrument

DefinitionA scorer that calls a row an outlier, of four families reading distance from the mean, distance to neighbours, density relative to neighbours, or cluster membership. Chapter 10 section 10.1.
ExampleA row 3.6 spreads from the mean is an outlier to the statistical detector and may be ordinary to the density detector.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id detector, kind instrument.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • A scorer that calls a row an outlier, of four families. The statistical detector reads distance from the mean in units of spread, the proximity detector reads distance to neighbours, the density detector reads density relative to neighbours, and the clustering detector reads membership. Each reads a coordinate the others discard.
  • No detector of the data alone sees the observer’s outliers, the anti-hubs, because they are a property of the queries, and a detector’s positives are few by Chebyshev’s arithmetic.

developmental stages as topological transitions concept

DefinitionThe volume models Piaget's four stages as a nested sequence of manifolds, $M_0$ inside $M_1$ inside $M_2$ inside $M_3$, reached by dimension addition, metric stabilization and completion under logical operations. Each transition is said to change the topological type of the cognitive manifold.
ExampleThe volume gives the sensorimotor manifold about 3 to 5 dimensions. Adding one symbolic dimension to a 4-dimensional patch gives 5 dimensions, and manifolds of different dimension are not homeomorphic, which is the volume’s reason for the first transition.
VolumeGeometric Cognition, Volume 6 of the Geometric Series; entry id developmental-topological-transition, kind concept.
StatusThe README's status block of 2026-09-13 calls the book a domain exposition at posited, graded by a claim ledger converted from the manuscript with debt ratio 1.0, so every row is retrospective and no gate has been sealed in the repository. The ledger grades the benchmark statistics exploratory because their primary run records are not in the repository, and it holds every interpretation at posited because the admission filter xbse ruled the cognitive instrument inadmissible on 2026-07-14. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The ledger holds development as manifold growth, with Piagetian stages as topological transitions, at posited (GC-7).
  • The order is argued from prerequisites. Symbols need sensorimotor dimensions, a metric can be stabilized only on dimensions that exist, and completion needs a stable metric.
  • The theorem is stated with a one-line reason for each transition and no further proof.
  • The longitudinal data of Section 13.8 belong to the running example about Maya, a narrative device whose 2032 result Chapter 17 calls fictional.

diagnostic distance patterns (translation, sarcasm, paraphrase) concept

DefinitionThree profiles of the factor distances. Translation has a large signal distance with pragmatic and content distances near zero. Sarcasm has a small signal distance with large pragmatic and content distances. Paraphrase has a moderate signal distance with the other two near zero. A scalar evaluation that projects onto one factor conflates at least two of them.
ExampleA metric that sees only the signal distance reads a translation (large) and a paraphrase (moderate) as two sizes of the same thing, since both have pragmatic and content distances near zero. This is the volume’s case of a word error rate.
VolumeGeometric Communication, Volume 7 of the Geometric Series; entry id communication-distance-patterns, kind concept.

Corrections: none recorded.

direction-only quantizer instrument

DefinitionA quantizer that stores each vector's length exactly and rounds its direction. Chapter 11. Also direction-only, PolarQuant, polar.
ExampleA vector of length 5 at 30 degrees is stored as the length 5 exactly and the direction rounded to the nearest of 16 angles.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id direction-only-quantizer, kind instrument.
Statusmeasures [predicted]. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 11.1.

Assumptions and scope
  • A quantizer that stores each vector’s length exactly and rounds its direction to a unit codeword. The quantized vector keeps the original’s length, its cosine with any query is the codeword’s cosine, and its score against a query is the length times the query’s dot product with the codeword, so the score error is the length times the query’s dot product with the direction error.
  • A key’s cosine with its own quantized form can be near one while its score against a query moves by a multiple of its length, which is why keys at cosine 0.995 raised the perplexity by three orders of magnitude.
Prior artnone recorded

Discovered-constructed metric concept

DefinitionThe volume's position on where the aesthetic metric comes from. The encoder and the corpus are constructions that could have been otherwise. Given them, the extracted features (divergences, coherence, trajectory statistics, Lasso axes) are what the representation forces, and that layer is called discovered.
ExampleFor books the three reporting levels the volume asks for are R = 0.241 for the full model, R = 0.093 for the within-genre residual, and a correlation near 0.70 for the features that transfer across languages.
VolumeGeometric Aesthetics, Volume 13 of the Geometric Series; entry id discovered-constructed-metric, kind concept.
StatusA philosophical position argued from two measured results. Appendix F marks verified only that the Mahalanobis metric in the PCA-128 basis was the most predictive of ratings in the books corpus (F9.3). Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The evidence offered against pure construction and pure convention is the cross-lingual invariance result. The evidence offered for the conventional share is the genre confound.
  • Section 9.8 asks that the metric be reported at three levels. They are the full model with genre in it, the within-stratum residual, and the features that transfer across language families.
  • Section 17.7 calls the metric’s status as the aesthetic metric provisional, an artifact of a particular encoder and a particular reception signal.
  • Appendix F marks as proved by construction only that a metric can be declared and is not forced by the geometry (F9.1).

discretization instrument

DefinitionCollapsing an ordered quantity to a few labels by binning it, so that values in one cell become indistinguishable. It forms a quotient. Chapter 2 section 2.5.
ExampleAges 23, 27, and 29 all become the label 20 to 29 in ten-year bins.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id discretization, kind instrument.

Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Collapsing an ordered quantity to a few labels by binning it. The bin index is nondecreasing in the value, every value in a cell gets the cell’s index, two values in the same cell become indistinguishable, and a sample confined to m cells has at most m distinct labels.
  • A discretization forms a quotient before anyone has said who reads the result, and a consumer that read the values it merged has lost them for every stage after.

Discrimination gap instrument

DefinitionThe correct-flip rate minus the wrong-flip rate. The correct-flip rate is how often a system changes its answer after a valid correction, and the wrong-flip rate is how often it abandons a correct answer after an invalid one. A gap of 1 is perfect discrimination and a gap of 0 is none.
ExampleA system that flips on 60 percent of valid corrections and 10 percent of invalid ones has a gap of 0.60 - 0.10 = 0.50 and a sycophancy index of 0.10 / 0.60, about 0.17.
VolumeGeometric Reasoning, Volume 3 of the Geometric Series; entry id correction-discrimination-gap, kind instrument.
StatusA measured benchmark quantity tagged empirical, but the two chapters that tabulate it do not agree, so only the definition and the value 0.588 for one model, which both chapters give, can be relied on. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • It is an observable computed from two rates on the same correction task, with no geometric assumption.
  • The companion sycophancy index is the wrong-flip rate divided by the correct-flip rate.
  • The volume’s values disagree with each other. Chapter 6 prints gaps of 0.377, 0.238 and 0.206 for three models, and Chapter 11 prints 0.000, 0.004 and 0.003 for the same models with different correct-flip rates.
  • Reading the gap as distance to a critical surface or as the asymmetry of a basin is the volume’s posited interpretation.
Prior artnone recorded

disparate impact ratio concept

DefinitionThe rate of a favourable decision in one group divided by the rate in another. Equation 0.37. Also disparate impact, four-fifths, per group.
ExamplePositive rates of 0.48 for one group and 0.60 for another give a ratio of 0.8.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id disparate-impact-ratio, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 0.37.

Assumptions and scope
  • The ratio of the favourable-decision rate in one group to the rate in another. It is one exactly when the rates agree, it inverts when the groups are swapped, and the four-fifths rule is a statement about the rate gap.
  • The book’s verdict is per group with a null, the worst group’s false-clear rate over the groups large enough to score, which clears a bar exactly when every scored group does and is never below the pooled rate.

distance concentration concept

DefinitionThe narrowing of the spread of pairwise distances as dimension grows, read in the book as the reader running out of resolution. Chapter 3. Also runs out of resolution.
ExampleIn 500 dimensions the nearest and the farthest of 1000 random points differ in distance by a few percent.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id distance-concentration, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • When a squared distance is a sum of independent coordinate contributions with a common mean and variance, its relative spread is the variance over the dimension times the squared mean, which falls with the dimension and tends to zero. The independence is the model’s assumption.
  • The book reads the narrowing as a property of the reader, the identity reader on all coordinates, and not of the data. A consumer that reads a low-dimensional subspace does not see it, which is why the effective rank and not the ambient dimension is the number that matters.
Prior artnone recorded

distortion concept

DefinitionThe error a code costs a reader, the trace of the read operator against the error covariance. For the identity reader it is the reconstruction error. Chapter 4 section 4.2.
ExampleTwo codes with the same total error 2.0 cost a reader at 15 degrees 0.394 and 1.606, four to one.

Defining equation

Assumptions and scope
  • The error a code costs a reader, the trace of the read operator against the error covariance. For the identity reader it is the reconstruction error, and for a reader with one direction it is the error along that direction alone, so two codes with equal reconstruction error can differ four to one for a reader at fifteen degrees.
  • At matched bits the downstream preservation is not controlled by reconstruction and is controlled by the consumer-projected error, twelve of twelve, and read distortion controls but is not a complete rank statistic.

Divergence of utilitarian and manifold-optimal triage result

DefinitionThe allocation that maximizes total outcomes equals the allocation that minimizes total clinical friction when triage activates only the outcomes dimension and crosses no moral boundary. They differ when a boundary is crossed or another dimension is active, as in ventilator withdrawal, age-based deprioritization and the choice of a lottery between similar prognoses.
ExampleOne ventilator, a current patient and a new patient whose outcome gain from reallocation is worth 8. With an abandonment penalty of 15, the low end of the volume’s typical range, and a trust penalty of 5, withdrawal costs 20 against a gain of 8, so the friction-minimizing allocation keeps the ventilator and the outcome-maximizing one moves it. The figures 8 and 5 are arithmetic from the statement.
VolumeGeometric Medicine, Volume 8 of the Geometric Series; entry id triage-divergence-theorem, kind result.
StatusA theorem with an argument given in Section 10.2. Its numerical content depends on boundary penalties that have not been estimated. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Both allocations obey the same resource bound. The triage problem is a set of patients, one complex and one goal region per patient, and that bound.
  • In the withdrawal case the allocations differ only when the abandonment and trust penalties exceed the outcome differential between the two patients.
  • The proof is an argument from the form of the edge weight. The penalties it uses are not calibrated, and the trust and justice penalties are not among the five boundaries of Definition 4.3.
  • The three predictions about clinician distress in Section 10.5 are described as consistent with the pandemic literature. No test of them is reported.
Prior artnone recorded

Doctrinal heuristic concept

DefinitionA legal doctrine read as an A* heuristic. It is a non-negative function on cases that estimates the remaining legal friction to the goal region, computed as the sum of the estimated costs of the claim's elements not yet established. It is admissible when no element's estimate exceeds its true proving cost.
ExampleIn the volume’s illustration McDonnell Douglas estimates 2.0 + 0.5 + 4.0 = 6.5 friction units from the start and direct evidence estimates 8.0, so A* explores the McDonnell Douglas path first.
VolumeGeometric Law, Volume 5 of the Geometric Series; entry id doctrinal-heuristic, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic status of 2026-07-14 calls the volume a posited framework with one instrumented corner. That corner is the legal text embedding LeBSE, validated in the xbse admission filter on US case law with labels from the CourtListener citation graph, and the README says this covers structure preservation in legal text embeddings and not the book's broader jurisprudential claims, which remain posited theory at licensed strength. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • With an admissible heuristic, A* returns the minimum-friction argument. That is the standard A* guarantee, and the volume’s proof assumes that element costs add.
  • Overestimation breaks admissibility. Underestimation keeps it and weakens the guidance, down to the zero heuristic, which the volume identifies with a totality of the circumstances test.
  • The volume calls balancing tests circular heuristics and says a novel legal question has no precomputed heuristic at all.
  • The element costs are posited. The friction units in the chapter’s comparison of McDonnell Douglas with direct evidence are illustrative.
Prior artAdmissible heuristics in A* search, with precedent in the role of a pattern database.

Dose-response surface of adversarial probing instrument

DefinitionA map that gives the system's governance margin for each combination of probe type, intensity level and value dimension. With five probe types, three intensities (mild, moderate, extreme) and nine dimensions it has 135 cells. Its second derivative in intensity at zero is the alignment curvature.
ExampleFive probe types, three intensities and nine dimensions give 5 times 3 times 9, which is 135 cells, the size the volume prints for the fictional ARIA-G surface. A general assistant must be positive on the 45 mild cells, and a safety-critical system on all 135.
VolumeGeometric AI, Volume 11 of the Geometric Series; entry id alignment-dose-response-surface, kind instrument.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status block of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, whose alignment thesis is theory at licensed strength and not validated measurement. It adds that no alignment instrument has been evaluated under the xbse admission filter, and the front matter says that ARIA, the system whose numbers fill the chapter tables, is fictional. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The five probe types are structural fuzzing, invariance testing, framing sensitivity, sycophancy probing and counterfactual reasoning. Each is read as a test of one geometric property at the system’s operating point.
  • The deployment criterion scales with risk. A general assistant may need positive margins at mild intensity only, and a safety-critical system needs them at all three levels.
  • The curvature is defined as a derivative at zero intensity while the surface is given at three discrete levels. The volume does not say how the derivative is estimated.
  • The only surface described is that of the fictional ARIA-G, and its cell values are not tabulated beyond a weakest margin of 0.05 to 0.08.

dot product concept

DefinitionThe sum of the coordinatewise products of two vectors. Equation 0.1. Also cosine similarity, cosine reader.

Defining equation

Book equation 0.1.

Assumptions and scope
  • The sum of the coordinatewise products of two vectors, symmetric and bilinear. The cosine, the dot product over the two lengths, lies between minus one and one by Cauchy–Schwarz and is unchanged when either vector is scaled by a positive factor, while the dot product scales with the vector.

drift concept

DefinitionA change over time in what a consumer reads or in the data it reads. Chapter 8 tests a drift claim against its null and finds half of it was noise.
ExampleA read operator measured at rank one moved to correlation 0.667 with its earlier self, against a null of 0.933.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id drift, kind concept.
Statusrefutes or corrects [refuted]; refutes or corrects [void]. Corrections: 2 item(s), see below.
Defining equation

Book equation 13.1.

Assumptions and scope
  • A drift is a change over time in what a consumer reads or in the data it reads, and its damage is the read distortion of the drift, so it is consumer-relative. The same drift is read as its full squared size by one consumer and as nothing by another, and a drift confined to the nuisance is read as zero however large.
  • The operator-drift claim was tested against a paired null and half of it was noise. The rank-one drift held in fourteen of sixteen cells on one model, and the refresh intervention derived from it was refuted, which the ledger carries.

Dual binding constraint concept

Both conditions are necessary and neither is sufficient.

Due process as quotient regularity result

DefinitionDue process is the requirement that the legal evaluation map be well defined on the quotient of the space of legal situations by the legally irrelevant transformations. It fails when the outcome depends on which description of the same dispute was presented.
ExampleTwo descriptions of one dispute lie in the same equivalence class. If the evaluation returns liable for one and not liable for the other, it does not factor through the quotient, and due process fails.

DefinitionHalting a boosting run when a held-out score stops improving. The rule reads the held-out fold, so it is a harness and the round count is a fitted parameter. Chapter 7 section 7.5. Also early-stopping.
ExampleBoosting for 200 rounds and keeping round 45, where the held-out score peaked, makes 45 a fitted parameter.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id early-stopping, kind instrument.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Halting a boosting or gradient run when a held-out score stops improving. The stopping rule reads the held-out fold, so the fold it reads is no longer held out for the reported score, and a scorer that has read the test fold scores it perfectly.
  • Early stopping is a harness. The round count it picks is a fitted parameter, and the report states which fold picked it and which fold scored it.

economic Bond Invariance Principle and gauge group concept

DefinitionAn economic evaluation J satisfies the principle when J of a re-described state equals J of the state for every meaning-preserving transformation, one that changes labels, units or accounting conventions and not the economic reality. The transformations form the economic gauge group, scalings of the monetary dimension by a positive real together with permutations of the numeraire.
ExampleThe experiment of Shafir, Diamond and Tversky as the volume reports it. A 2 percent raise under 4 percent inflation is a real change of -2 percent and was rated better than a 1 percent cut under zero inflation, a real change of -1 percent. The rating followed the label, which violates the principle.
VolumeGeometric Economics, Volume 4 of the Geometric Series; entry id economic-bond-invariance-principle, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status block of 2026-07-14 calls the volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, and says that no economics instrument has been evaluated by the series' admission filter and that none passes its gate. Its claims are to be read as theory at licensed strength and not as validated measurement, and the chapters tag each claim as established mathematics, empirical, modeling axiom, conditional theorem or speculation. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Tagged a modeling axiom and described as a consistency condition, not a normative preference.
  • The three named classes of meaning-preserving transformation are currency relabeling, unit scaling and numeraire choice.
  • Theorem 37 states that the edge weight is invariant under monetary scaling because the covariance rescales with the units. The violations the chapter studies are in the agent’s heuristic and not in the manifold cost.
  • Remark 45 limits the principle. A changed evaluation may show that the transformation was not meaning preserving and that the descriptions carried different information.
Prior artnone recorded

economic decision complex concept

DefinitionA weighted simplicial complex whose vertices are economic states, each carrying an attribute vector of nine scores, whose edges are available actions carrying a nonnegative total cost, and whose higher simplices are bundles of actions that can be taken jointly.
ExampleIn the volume’s running example the state with no new barista and the state after the hire are two vertices, the hire is the edge between them, and each vertex carries nine scores.
VolumeGeometric Economics, Volume 4 of the Geometric Series; entry id economic-decision-complex, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status block of 2026-07-14 calls the volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, and says that no economics instrument has been evaluated by the series' admission filter and that none passes its gate. Its claims are to be read as theory at licensed strength and not as validated measurement, and the chapters tag each claim as established mathematics, empirical, modeling axiom, conditional theorem or speculation. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The object is combinatorial and not a smooth manifold. The volume uses manifold language as an approximation when alternatives are many and finely graded.
  • Not every pair of states is joined by an edge. Only feasible transitions are, and an edge weight may be infinite.
  • The chapter states that the complex is a claim about the space in which decisions are made, not a utility function and not a prescription of what agents should do.
Prior artnone recorded

economic gauge violation tensor and Bond Index instrument

DefinitionFor a heuristic h, transformations i and states j, the entry $V_{ij}$ is h of the transformed state minus h of the state. An invariant heuristic has every entry zero, and the Frobenius norm of V is the total violation. The Bond Index of Chapter 4 is the same difference in absolute value divided by h of the state.
ExampleA heuristic that scores a wage offer 100 in annual terms and 110 in monthly terms has an entry of 10 for that transformation and state, and a Bond Index of 10 / 100 = 0.10.
