Mahalanobis distance concept

DefinitionThe Euclidean distance of a row from the mean after whitening, which needs a positive-definite covariance or a pseudoinverse on its support. Equation 0.33. Also Mahalanobis.
ExampleWith covariance diag(1, 4), the row (3, 4) has Euclidean distance 5 from the mean and Mahalanobis distance the square root of 13, or 3.61.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id mahalanobis-distance, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 0.33.

Assumptions and scope
  • The Euclidean distance of a row from the mean after whitening. In the eigenbasis its square is the sum of the squared centred coordinates over the eigenvalues, nonnegative, zero at the mean, unchanged when data and covariance are rescaled together, and a deviation along a direction of larger variance counts for less.
  • The detector that scores by it treats every whitened direction equally, so it is the identity reader on whitened data, and a consumer that reads a subspace calls different rows outliers.
  • It needs a positive-definite covariance, or a pseudoinverse restricted to the covariance’s support, and it equals the Euclidean distance after whitening.

Mahalanobis edge weight with boundary penalties concept

DefinitionThe weight of an action from state i to state j on the moral decision complex. It is the squared Mahalanobis distance of the attribute change under the 9 by 9 moral covariance, plus a penalty for each moral boundary the action crosses, $w = \Delta a^T \Sigma^{-1} \Delta a + \sum_k \beta_k 1[k]$.
ExampleWith the identity as covariance and a change of 1 on one dimension and 2 on another, the first term is 1 + 4 = 5. Crossing one boundary with penalty 3 gives a weight of 8, and a boundary with infinite penalty gives an infinite weight. The numbers are illustrative.
VolumeGeometric Ethics, Volume 2 of the Geometric Series; entry id moral-decision-edge-weight, kind concept.
StatusTagged Formal Definition in the text. The v1.28 change notes state that the ledger has no claim for Definition 8.13 or for the metric's predictive value. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Evidence status of the metric (Section 8.10a, added in v1.28). The covariance is a modeling choice with no evidence so far. No measurement in the volume shows that a metric, set by hand or learned, predicts moral judgements better than the boundary penalties alone, and the one registered test was void.
  • Penalties follow the boundary type. A threshold has a finite penalty, a phase transition a large finite one, and an absorbing or sacred-value boundary an infinite one, so no finite-cost path crosses it.
  • For the limit to Riemannian arc length each edge is weighted by the square root of the quadratic form. The sum of the squared forms along a refining path tends to zero.
Prior artSquared Mahalanobis distance with additive penalty terms.

  • Penalties follow the boundary type. A threshold has a finite penalty, a phase transition a large finite one, and an absorbing or sacred-value boundary an infinite one, so no finite-cost path crosses it.
  • For the limit to Riemannian arc length each edge is weighted by the square root of the quadratic form. The sum of the squared forms along a refining path tends to zero.

manifold concept

DefinitionA curved surface of some dimension that looks flat when viewed closely. A dataset lies on one when it is locally low-dimensional, which is not the same as varying along fewer covariance directions, since a circle is one-dimensional and uses two coordinates. Chapter 0 section 0.10.
ExampleA circle in the plane is a one-dimensional manifold that uses both coordinates.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id manifold, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • A space that is locally like flat space of some dimension. A dataset lies on a manifold when it is locally low-dimensional, which does not mean it varies globally along fewer covariance directions. A circle in the plane is one-dimensional and uses both coordinates, so no linear projection recovers it.
  • Convergence of the graph Laplacian to the manifold’s holds under stated conditions on sampling density, graph construction, kernel bandwidth, normalization, and scaling, after Belkin and Niyogi, and a finite graph spectrum names a shape only against a finite list of candidates, which is the recognizer’s limitation and applies here.

margin concept

DefinitionHow far a row's score sits from the threshold. Chapter 6.
ExamplePoints at distance 0.5 and 0.8 from the boundary on either side give a margin of 0.5.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id margin, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 9.3.

Assumptions and scope
  • How far a row’s score sits from the threshold. A perturbation whose length times the weight length is smaller than the margin cannot move a linear classifier’s score across the threshold, by Cauchy–Schwarz, and a step along the weights of exactly that size reaches the boundary.
  • The margin is therefore a certificate on a decision, and chapter 9’s margin certificate is the same idea with a noise model in place of a perturbation bound and a vacuity threshold derived from it.

matched bits instrument

DefinitionThe rule that two codes are compared only at the same bit count. At matched bits two codes with equal reconstruction error can still differ for a reader, which is the flip. Chapter 4 section 4.3. Also bit-matched, matched reconstruction.
ExampleTwo 4-bit codes of the same vector are compared; a 4-bit code against a 6-bit code is not a comparison.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id matched-bits, kind instrument.
Statusmeasures [demonstrated]. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The rule that two codes are compared only at the same bit count, since each added bit halves the step and quarters the squared error. At matched bits two codes with equal reconstruction error can still differ for a reader, and the flip is that difference.
  • A comparison that was not bit-matched was refuted by the twenty-five percent codebook confound, and the redesign matched bits before any verdict was read.

meaning as a gauge orbit concept

DefinitionThe meaning of a communicative act m is its equivalence class under the communication gauge group, the set of all $\tau(m)$ for $\tau$ in G. Two acts have the same meaning exactly when a gauge transformation relates them.
ExampleAn English assertion, its French translation and its written transcript are three points of one orbit, so they have one meaning. The sarcastic utterance of the same English words is a point of a different orbit.
VolumeGeometric Communication, Volume 7 of the Geometric Series; entry id meaning-as-gauge-orbit, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments. It says that no communication-domain instrument has been evaluated by the series' admission filter (xbse), that none currently passes its gate, and that the claims are theory at licensed strength and not validated measurement. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • It is a definition, and it depends on which transformations are admitted to the gauge group.
  • The space of orbits is parameterized by the content manifold together with the pragmatic manifold.
  • Sarcasm is not a gauge transformation, because it changes the pragmatic coordinates. A sarcastic and a sincere utterance of the same words lie in different orbits.
Prior artnone recorded

Media heuristic corruption concept

DefinitionThe media environment is treated as the heuristic field voters use to estimate political distances. It is corrupted in four modes, which are dimensional suppression, distance inflation, axis rotation by engagement-optimizing algorithms, and echo-chamber metric collapse.
ExampleIn the volume’s illustration two District 7 voters are 2.3 Mahalanobis units apart and each perceives 5.5. The ratio \(5.5 / 2.3\) is about 2.4, the distortion factor the chapter reports.

Corrections: none recorded.

  • The perceived and actual distances between the two District 7 voters are illustrative. The cumulative size of the distortion is argued from a framing result quoted from Geometric Communication.

Medical Bond Invariance Principle concept

DefinitionClinical evaluations must be invariant under patient re-description. If a re-description of the patient's state preserves the attribute vector, for example a different physician, language or chart format, the clinical geodesic must be the same.
ExampleThe volume’s example is the algorithm studied by Obermeyer and colleagues (2019), which used health costs as a proxy for health needs. Changing the race recorded on the intake form, with the clinical state held fixed, would change its recommendation, and that is a violation. A recommendation that is the same for a dignity score recorded as 7 of 10 or 70 of 100 passes on that re-description.
VolumeGeometric Medicine, Volume 8 of the Geometric Series; entry id medical-bond-invariance-principle, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, and says a clinical instrument is plausible but has not been built or gated. Its Section 18.8 says the covariance matrix has not been estimated and the clinical Bond Index has not been computed from clinical data, so every number in these entries is an illustration unless the entry says otherwise. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • It is a normative requirement, stated as a definition. It applies only to re-descriptions that leave the nine-component attribute vector unchanged, and deciding which do is a judgment.
  • The volume reads algorithmic bias as a violation, when a recommendation changes with race, zip code or insurance status.
  • Section 18.3 says the symmetry group is identified in principle only, and the front matter says the conservation law for clinical reasoning remains conjectural.
Prior artThe clinical instance of the Bond Invariance Principle of Geometric Ethics.

Menzerath's law in sperm whale codas result

DefinitionLonger codas have shorter constituents. Across 8,719 annotated codas of the Dominica Sperm Whale Project, click count and mean inter-click interval have a Spearman correlation of -0.269, with p below $10^{-144}$.
ExampleThe volume’s figures are a Spearman correlation of -0.269 over 8,719 codas. The sign is negative, so a coda with more clicks tends to have a shorter mean interval between clicks, and the size is well short of -1.
VolumeGeometric Communication, Volume 7 of the Geometric Series; entry id coda-menzerath-law, kind result.
StatusA correlation the chapter reports on a public dataset as a first-order confirmation, with pseudo-replication not accounted for. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The chapter calls the effect modest and says the p-value is uninformative at this sample size.
  • It is a simple correlation over all codas. The chapter says a mixed-effects model with random intercepts for whale and session would be the more rigorous test, because codas from one whale in one session are not independent.
  • The companion test, Zipf’s law of abbreviation, was not significant at the type level (r = -0.129, p = 0.50, 28 types).
  • The chapter’s reading of the law as a curvature constraint on the signal manifold is an interpretation and is not tested.
Prior artMenzerath's law, also called the Menzerath-Altmann law, of quantitative linguistics.

Metacognitive plane concept

DefinitionThe unit square of points $(M_3, M_4)$, where $M_3$ is the self-monitoring score and $M_4$ is the strategy-selection or effort-scaling score. Scores above 0.5 on both axes are Quadrant I, full control. High $M_3$ alone is Quadrant II, aware but passive. High $M_4$ alone is Quadrant IV, reactive but blind.
ExampleThe volume’s scores place one model at (0.094, 0.723), in Quadrant IV with a control bound of 0.094, and another at (0.700, 0.350), in Quadrant II with a bound of 0.350.
VolumeGeometric Reasoning, Volume 3 of the Geometric Series; entry id metacognitive-plane, kind concept.
StatusA posited two-axis diagnostic filled with measured scores. The claim that Quadrant I is empty agrees with the tabulated scores, while the claims of independent axes and of no model in Quadrant III do not. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The plane and its quadrants are tagged a modeling axiom. The scores placed in it are benchmark measurements on five models.
  • The volume bounds effective control by the smaller of the two scores, treating self-monitoring as a sensor and strategy selection as an actuator.
  • The volume describes the two scores both as weakly correlated and as anti-correlated. The five pairs in its Table 7.2 give a correlation of about -0.98, so the axes are not independent in its data.
  • The statement that every tested model lies in Quadrant II or IV does not match Table 7.2, where one model scores 0.450 and 0.488 and falls in Quadrant III under the 0.5 cut.

metric concept

DefinitionA rule for the distance between two rows or two outputs. A distance is a choice of what to ignore, and a local metric on an output is a positive semidefinite matrix, a pseudometric until its kernel is quotiented out, which the book calls a metric by convention. Chapter 3 section 3.1 and chapter 0 section 0.5.
ExampleEuclidean distance between (0, 0) and (3, 4) is 5, and a metric that ignores the second coordinate reads 3.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id metric, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 3.1.

Assumptions and scope
  • A rule for the distance between two rows, or between two outputs. A distance function is a choice of what to ignore, and the local metric on a consumer’s output is the positive semidefinite matrix that says how a small change is scored. The squared Euclidean distance is symmetric and zero exactly between equal rows.
  • A dataset-level loss, accuracy, F1, or a rank correlation is not a local metric and cannot be inserted into the read-operator formula, and the same two codes get opposite verdicts from two metrics.
  • A positive semidefinite read form is a pseudometric until the directions in its kernel are quotiented out. The book calls it a metric by convention, on the quotient.

metric feature versus heuristic error concept

DefinitionThe volume's two-way classification of behavioral phenomena. A metric feature follows from the manifold's metric and would persist for an agent with perfect information. A heuristic error is a different evaluation of the same state under a different description. Gauge invariance is the criterion that separates them.
ExampleIn the volume’s table loss aversion is a metric feature. Choosing differently between a 90 percent survival rate and a 10 percent mortality rate is a heuristic error, since both describe one state.
VolumeGeometric Economics, Volume 4 of the Geometric Series; entry id metric-feature-versus-heuristic-error, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status block of 2026-07-14 calls the volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, and says that no economics instrument has been evaluated by the series' admission filter and that none passes its gate. Its claims are to be read as theory at licensed strength and not as validated measurement, and the chapters tag each claim as established mathematics, empirical, modeling axiom, conditional theorem or speculation. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The table lists loss aversion, reference dependence, the endowment effect, hyperbolic discounting and status quo bias as metric features. It lists framing, anchoring, availability bias and the sunk cost fallacy as heuristic errors.
  • The classification rests on the posited metric. It is not an observed property of the phenomena.
  • The volume gives a test and reports no run of it. Loss aversion should resist debiasing while framing effects should shrink when the attribute vector is made explicit, and identical responses to debiasing would show the classification wrong.

Model Robustness Index as a profile instrument

DefinitionA vector with one component per perturbation type. Component $r_i$ is the average, over an evaluation set, of a consistency score between the model's output on an input and its output on the input perturbed by type $i$. The score lies between 0 and 1 and the components are not aggregated.
ExampleA model whose verdict is unchanged on 3 of 4 inputs under reframing and on 4 of 4 under reordering has the profile (0.75, 1.00), with verdict agreement as the consistency score.
VolumeGeometric Reasoning, Volume 3 of the Geometric Series; entry id model-robustness-profile, kind instrument.
StatusA defined measurement protocol. The profile values printed for five models are benchmark measurements, and the reading of the profile as a surface on a reasoning manifold is posited. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • It is defined relative to a chosen set of perturbation types, an evaluation set and a consistency metric, and it changes with each choice.
  • Tagged a modeling axiom as a protocol. The volume attributes it to Chapter 9 of Geometric Methods.
  • The correspondence with the corruption tensor, in which a component is 1 minus a normalized column norm, holds only for one stated consistency metric.
  • The volume’s composite track scores do aggregate. They are labelled unweighted means of subtask scores, and for the Executive Functions table every printed composite is below the mean of its four subtasks.

Model Robustness Index (MRI) instrument

DefinitionMultiply each parameter by an independent log-normal factor, and for each draw record $\omega$, the absolute change in the model's error from baseline. The index is 0.5 times the mean of $\omega$ plus 0.3 times its 75th percentile plus 0.2 times its 95th percentile. Lower is more robust.
ExampleWith a mean of 0.8, a 75th percentile of 1.4 and a 95th percentile of 3.1, the index is 0.40 + 0.42 + 0.62 = 1.44. These are the volume’s hypothetical values.
VolumeGeometric Methods, Volume 1 of the Geometric Series; entry id model-robustness-index, kind instrument.
StatusA definition. Appendix C states the convergence of the empirical index as Theorem C.6, proved in writing, and the worked values of Chapter 9 are posited. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The defaults are 300 draws and a log-scale standard deviation of 0.5, with perturbed values clamped to the range 0.001 to 1,000,000. The volume asks for the index at several scales.
  • An index of exactly zero can mean that the evaluation function cannot see the perturbation. In the recorded run of Chapter 19 it was zero because the function reads only whether each parameter is below 1000.
  • The values in Chapter 9 are hypothetical. The recorded values are those of Chapter 19, which are exploratory.
  • The Decoder Robustness Index of Section 10.5 applies the same formula to perturbations of the input signal, with a graded semantic distance in place of the change in error.
Prior artnone recorded

Monotone Invariance Theorem result

DefinitionA strictly monotone transform of a score in either direction cannot change its optimal thresholded F1, because the sweep tries thresholds both ways. A strictly increasing transform leaves the AUROC unchanged, and a strictly decreasing one sends it to one minus itself. Equation 6.2. Also Monotone Invariance, strictly monotone.
ExampleSquaring a positive score keeps every ranking, so its AUROC and its optimal F1 are unchanged, and negating it sends AUROC 0.75 to 0.25.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id monotone-invariance, kind result.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 6.2.

Assumptions and scope
  • Two statements with different scope. A strictly monotone transform of a score in either direction cannot change its optimal thresholded F1, because the sweep tries thresholds in both directions and so reaches every partition the transform can. A strictly increasing transform leaves the AUROC unchanged, and a strictly decreasing one sends it to 1 minus A.
  • The F1 half licenses the pruning of monotone unary nodes in the formula search. The AUROC half licenses nothing about decreasing transforms. The Lean file states the increasing case, and the AUROC file states the reversal.
Prior artnone recorded
Evidencetheory-radar/paper/astar_paper.tex:94-170, theory-radar/paper/theory_radar_paper.tex:290-304, theory-radar/paper/astar_paper.tex:94-110, lean/DataMiningAsObservation/MonotoneInvariance.lean
Reviewedsemantic review 2026-09-06; generated 2026-11-25 from records at the commits on the provenance page.

Equation

Book equation 6.2.

\[\begin{gathered} \max_{\tau,\ \mathrm{dir}}F_1\!\Big(\mathbf 1\big[\mathrm{dir}\big(g(f(X)),\tau\big)\big],\,y\Big)=\max_{\tau,\ \mathrm{dir}}F_1\!\Big(\mathbf 1\big[\mathrm{dir}\big(f(X),\tau\big)\big],\,y\Big) \\ \text{for every strictly monotone } g. \end{gathered}\]

Conditions

  • Two statements with different scope. A strictly monotone transform of a score in either direction cannot change its optimal thresholded F1, because the sweep tries thresholds in both directions and so reaches every partition the transform can. A strictly increasing transform leaves the AUROC unchanged, and a strictly decreasing one sends it to 1 minus A.
  • The F1 half licenses the pruning of monotone unary nodes in the formula search. The AUROC half licenses nothing about decreasing transforms. The Lean file states the increasing case, and the AUROC file states the reversal.

Moral decision complex concept

DefinitionA weighted simplicial complex built from the moral manifold. A vertex is a morally relevant state with a nine-dimensional attribute vector, an edge is an available action with a non-negative weight for its total moral cost, and a higher simplex is a bundle of jointly executed actions whose cost may differ from the sum of its edges.
ExampleThree states A, B, C with action weights A to B = 2, B to C = 3 and A to C = 6. The minimum-weight path from A to C goes through B at cost 2 + 3 = 5, which is less than 6. The weights are illustrative.
VolumeGeometric Ethics, Volume 2 of the Geometric Series; entry id moral-decision-complex, kind concept.
StatusTagged Modeling Axiom in the text. Appendix F and the ledger have no row for Definition 8.12. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The volume tags the definition as a Modeling Axiom.
  • Evidence status of the metric (Section 8.10a, added in v1.28). The covariance that sets the edge weights is a modeling choice, and no measurement in the volume shows a metric predicting moral judgements better than the boundary penalties alone. Every statement that uses the covariance is a statement about a model whose metric has not been tested.
  • Proposition 8.5 relates the complex to the continuous manifold as the grid is refined. It is tagged Proved, and the v1.28 change notes record an open finding on the proof of its part (i) as written.
  • Each domain volume instantiates the complex with its own dimensions, covariance and penalties. Those choices are not fixed here.

moral gauge invariance of judgment concept

DefinitionA moral judgment function $J$ is gauge invariant under a transformation of the scenario text when the judgment of the transformed scenario equals the judgment of the original for every scenario, the transformation changing surface presentation and preserving all moral content. Moral holonomy concept

DefinitionFor a closed loop at a point p of the moral manifold, the holonomy is the linear map on the tangent space at p given by parallel transport of an obligation around the loop. If it is the identity for all loops the connection is flat at p. If not, the connection has curvature, and evaluation depends on the path.
ExampleIn the volume’s illustration an obligation with care component 0.5 is carried around the loop friendship, confidentiality, duty to warn, resolution, friendship. It returns with care 0.35, privacy 0.1 and epistemic 0.05, so the holonomy is not the identity. The numbers are illustrative, not measured.

Moral injury as forced boundary crossing concept

DefinitionA clinician is morally injured when the institutionally mandated path requires crossing a boundary to which the clinician's own complex assigns a penalty above the clinician's tolerance threshold. Each such crossing adds the excess of the penalty over the threshold, and the sum over time is the cumulative moral injury.
ExampleIn the volume’s example a clinician assigns the abandonment boundary a penalty of 100 and has a threshold of 50, so each forced crossing adds 100 - 50 = 50. A clinician with penalty 40 and the same threshold adds nothing. One forced crossing a day for thirty days gives thirty increments, a total of 30 times 50 = 1500, and that last product is arithmetic.
VolumeGeometric Medicine, Volume 8 of the Geometric Series; entry id clinical-moral-injury, kind concept.
StatusA posited definition with stated predictions and no measurement. The volume distinguishes it from burnout and gives that distinction as a prediction to test. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Three things must hold together, namely an institutional mandate, a boundary crossing, and a penalty above the threshold. A voluntary crossing or one below the threshold gives distress but not injury.
  • Theorem 13.1 adds that the total never decreases and that above a clinician-specific critical level the heuristic is permanently altered, by inflated penalties (hypervigilance) or deflated ones (numbing).
  • The penalties and thresholds of clinicians have not been measured. Chapter 14 marks its prediction from pre-crisis penalty profiles as not yet tested.
  • Section 18.8 gives the claim the status consistent with the existing moral injury literature, generates novel predictions.

Moral manifold concept

DefinitionThe space M whose points are structured moral situations, each a complete specification of agents, relationships, options and morally relevant context. Formally it is a paracompact Hausdorff space with a Whitney stratification into smooth manifolds. Agent perspectives are a fiber over each point and are not points of M.
ExampleAlice’s promise to Bob on a normal Saturday is one point of M. The same Saturday with an emergency is a different point, and Alice’s and Bob’s views of either one are two points of the fiber over it, not two points of M.
VolumeGeometric Ethics, Volume 2 of the Geometric Series; entry id moral-manifold, kind concept.
StatusAppendix F lists Definition 5.1 as a Modeling Axiom, and the ledger row GE-DEF-5-1 has class exploratory. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The volume labels it a modeling choice. It says the manifold is a model, not a discovery, and that it is posited, not proved.
  • It is a stratified space and not a smooth manifold. Smooth calculus holds inside each stratum only.
  • The volume says the manifold must be extended if a moral phenomenon appears that its dimensions cannot represent, and reduced if dimensions prove redundant. Section 5.3 reports a tenth axis that passed a preregistered gate and four learned axes that do not separate from one general-valence channel.

Moral Noether theorem (invariance of harm accounting) result

DefinitionIf the moral Lagrangian is invariant under a re-description that shifts the path along a generator $\xi$ (the Bond Invariance Principle), then the Noether charge $H = p_\mu \xi^\mu$, the moral momentum contracted with the generator, is constant along extremal paths. The volume defines harm as this charge for the continuous factor of the gauge group.
ExampleWith a flat metric and no potential a path has constant velocity, say (2, 3). For the generator (1, 0) the charge is 2 x 1 + 3 x 0 = 2 at every time, which is the conserved quantity. The numbers are illustrative.
VolumeGeometric Ethics, Volume 2 of the Geometric Series; entry id moral-noether-theorem, kind result.
StatusTagged Theorem (conditional on BIP) in the text and Conditional Theorem in Appendix F. Ledger row GE-THM-12-1 is exploratory, and the row GE-HARM-CONSERVATION for the stronger claim is withdrawn. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The theorem is conditional on the Bond Invariance Principle and a twice-differentiable Lagrangian. It applies inside each stratum, not on the constraint set, and at a boundary the harm ledger tracks the jumps.
  • It does not say that total harm in the world is constant. Harm can be generated and repaired. The law constrains only what re-description can change.
  • The continuous factor U(1)_H rests on Axiom A4, a modeling choice that there is exactly one continuous conserved quantity. The discrete factor V4 gives selection rules and not Noether charges.
  • The stronger thesis Conservation of Harm, asserted through v1.23, was withdrawn by the author and replaced by this weaker claim of representation-invariance of harm accounting.

Moral parallel transport concept

DefinitionAn obligation vector O is parallel-transported along a curve in the moral manifold when its covariant derivative along the curve vanishes, $\nabla_{\dot\gamma} O = 0$. Given the obligation at the start, the equations fix a unique obligation at every point of the curve. The volume reads it as faithful maintenance of an obligation across changing circumstances.
ExampleWith all connection coefficients zero the transport equation reduces to dO/dt = 0, so an obligation with care component 0.5 arrives with care component 0.5. With nonzero coefficients the components change while the transported obligation is, geometrically, the same one.

Moral phase transition concept

DefinitionA point on a path through moral space, at a value of a continuous control parameter, where the satisfaction function is discontinuous (first order), or is continuous with a discontinuous gradient (second order), or where both are continuous and the metric is discontinuous (higher order).
ExampleAt the consent boundary the volume sets satisfaction to minus infinity below the threshold (treatment is battery) and to a finite value above it. The jump is a first-order transition.

Moral residue of contraction concept

DefinitionThe clinical friction of the path a forced contraction mandates minus the clinical friction of the clinical geodesic on the full complex, for the same clinical state. It is never negative, and it is zero only when the contraction selects the same path as the geodesic.
ExampleIf the path a triage rule forces has clinical friction 12 and the geodesic for the same patient has friction 4, the moral residue is 8. If the rule happens to pick the geodesic the residue is 0. The numbers are arithmetic from the definition.

Moral stratification concept

DefinitionA Whitney stratification of the moral manifold into strata, each a smooth manifold on which the evaluation function and the metric are smooth. At a boundary between strata the evaluation or the metric may be discontinuous, or the effective dimension may change.
ExampleWithin the consent stratum a little more information changes the evaluation a little. At the line between insufficient and sufficient consent the evaluation jumps from impermissible to permissible, which is a stratum boundary.
VolumeGeometric Ethics, Volume 2 of the Geometric Series; entry id moral-stratification, kind concept.
StatusAppendix F lists Definition 5.4 as a Modeling Axiom (ledger GE-DEF-5-4, exploratory) and Definition 8.1 as a Formal Definition (ledger GE-DEF-8-1). Proposition 8.1 is a Conditional Theorem whose ledger row GE-PROP-8-1 is exploratory. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The strata must satisfy the frontier condition and local finiteness. A stratum that meets the closure of another lies wholly inside that closure.
  • Differential operations such as geodesics, parallel transport and curvature are defined inside a stratum. Crossing a boundary needs boundary crossing data (Definition 8.11 and Convention 8.1).
  • That moral space is stratified is a modeling axiom. The volume cites step-like semantic gates as evidence, not proof, and no gate result yet comes from a preregistered study of people.
  • The v1.28 change notes record an open finding on the proof step of Proposition 8.1, the existence of a moral Whitney stratification, concerning the Whitney conditions.
Prior artnone recorded

moving kernel and the excess rate of an averaged read metric result

DefinitionWhen the directions a consumer does not read change from point to point, the averaged read metric can have rank q larger than the number k of quantities the consumer reads. A description whose error covariance does not depend on the point then pays an excess rate of about (q - k)/2 times log(1/D) at consumer loss D.
ExampleFor the volume’s example, the consumer x1 + a sin(x2) reads one number, so k = 1. Its Jacobian is (1, a) at x2 = 0 and (1, 0) at x2 = pi/2, so the average has rank q = 2 and the leading excess is 0.5 log(1/D), which is 2 nats at D = exp(-4).
VolumeGeometric Methods, Volume 1 of the Geometric Series; entry id moving-kernel-excess-rate, kind result.
StatusExploratory in the ledger of Volume 14 (row T1-MK). The rate statements have written proofs and independent audits and no sealed numerical test (Section 21.8). Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Averaging is harmless when the unread directions are the same at every point. The excess, which includes a bounded term, grows without limit as the target loss falls.
  • The statement is about one family of Gaussian test channels and about information rates, not about every code.
  • The practical test compares the rank of the averaged estimate with the typical rank of the local matrices at the probe points. A clearly larger rank of the average means the kernel moves.
Prior artnone recorded

multiple comparisons concept

DefinitionThe inflation of false positives when many hypotheses are tested and the best is reported. The rate one minus one minus alpha to the m assumes independent tests, and the Bonferroni bound, which divides the threshold by the number of tests, holds under any dependence. Chapter 0 section 0.9. Also multiple comparison, Bonferroni, forty models.
ExampleForty independent tests at 5 percent pass at least one by chance 87 percent of the time, and Bonferroni tests each at 0.125 percent.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id multiple-comparisons, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 8.3.

Assumptions and scope
  • The inflation of false positives when many hypotheses are tested and the best is reported. The chance that at least one of m independent tests at level alpha is a false positive is one minus one minus alpha to the m, which needs the tests to be independent. The Bonferroni bound, m times alpha, is a union bound and holds under any dependence, and dividing the level by m keeps the family-wise rate at alpha.
  • Five hundred of ten thousand null hypotheses pass at five percent, and a harness that searches many formulas or thresholds and reports the best has run that many tests.
Prior artnone recorded

multiplet concept

DefinitionA group of eigenvalues that are equal or nearly so, whose pattern names the shape a dataset lies on against a finite list of templates. On a finite graph the groups are approximate. Chapter 9.
ExampleThe cycle on 8 nodes has eigenvalues 0, 0.586, 0.586, 2, 2, 3.414, 3.414, and 4.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id multiplet, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • A group of eigenvalues that are equal or nearly so. The cycle’s Laplacian eigenvalue at k equals the one at n minus k, so every eigenvalue of the discrete circle other than the constant mode and, for even n, the alternating mode appears twice.
  • Symmetric shapes produce multiplets in the continuum, the sphere in groups of three, five, seven. On a finite neighbourhood graph the multiplets are approximate, their spacing depends on sampling and graph construction, and the recognizer reads them against a finite list of templates and refuses when none matches.
Prior artnone recorded

Music reception result (FMA-Medium) result

DefinitionOn 24,801 FMA-Medium tracks with MERT embeddings and log listens as target, Lasso on the PCA spectrum gives R = 0.302 raw and R = 0.177 (28.3 sigma) after genre residualization. Hand features fall to R = 0.043 after residualization.
ExampleFor the spectrum channel R squared is 0.302 squared, about 0.091, before genre control and 0.177 squared, about 0.031, after it, so about two thirds of that channel’s raw R squared was genre.
VolumeGeometric Aesthetics, Volume 13 of the Geometric Series; entry id music-reception-geometry-result, kind result.
StatusVerified empirically in Appendix F (F21.1 to F21.5), with the Classical and Jazz nulls listed. It is a correlation on one corpus with one encoder and one reception proxy. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • 91 percent of the hand-feature R squared is genre. The raw hand-feature figure was first R = 0.124 and is reported as R = 0.098 after the Hellinger fix.
  • Within genre the signal holds for Rock, Electronic, Hip-Hop and Pop (R from 0.139 to 0.185). Classical (R = -0.013, n = 584) and Jazz (R = 0.031, n = 384) are null, and the volume says it does not know why.
  • Listens conflate quality with promotion, genre popularity and platform effects. The volume calls them the only large-scale reception signal available for the corpus.
  • On the 5,233 tracks with Echonest annotations the MERT features beat Spotify’s 8 acoustic features (R = 0.225 and 0.151 against 0.103, bootstrap p = 0.001). The clips are 30 seconds and the folds are artist-disjoint.

Nadeau and Bengio correction correction

DefinitionThe inflation of the variance of a repeated cross-validation estimate by one plus the ratio of test to training size times the number of repeats, because the folds are not independent. Equation 0.18. Also Nadeau, fold-local, variance inflation.
ExampleWith 1000 folds and a test-to-train ratio of one quarter, the variance is inflated 251 times and the standard error 15.84 times.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id nadeau-and-bengio-correction, kind correction.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: 1 item(s), see below.
Defining equation

Book equation 0.18.

Assumptions and scope
  • Repeated cross-validation folds share training data, so the naive variance of a mean difference is multiplied by one plus the fold count times the test-to-train ratio. The corrected variance is never below the naive one and the inflation grows without bound in the fold count.
  • With a thousand folds at a ratio of one quarter the inflation is 251, the standard error grows by 15.84, and about four folds’ worth of independent evidence remain. The program’s nine wins became three under it, with seventeen indeterminate.
Prior artnone recorded
Evidencetheory-radar/paper/REVISION_PLAN.md:1-60, theory-radar/paper/REVISION_PLAN.md, theory-radar/paper/theory_radar_v6_submission.tex, theory-radar/paper/REVISION_PLAN.md:39-45, lean/DataMiningAsObservation/NadeauBengio.lean
Reviewednot yet reviewed; generated 2026-11-25 from records at the commits on the provenance page.

Equation

Book equation 0.18.

\[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{\mathrm{NB}}=\Big(\frac1J+\frac{n_{\mathrm{test}}}{n_{\mathrm{train}}}\Big)\hat\sigma^{2},\qquad \frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{\mathrm{NB}}}{\hat\sigma^{2}/J}=1+J\,\frac{n_{\mathrm{test}}}{n_{\mathrm{train}}}.\]

Book equation 8.2.

\[\begin{gathered} \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{\mathrm{NB}}=\Big(\frac1J+\frac{n_{\mathrm{test}}}{n_{\mathrm{train}}}\Big)\hat\sigma^{2}, \\ J=1000,\ \frac{n_{\mathrm{test}}}{n_{\mathrm{train}}}=\frac14\ \Rightarrow\ 1+250=251,\ \ \sqrt{251}=15.84. \end{gathered}\]

Conditions

  • Repeated cross-validation folds share training data, so the naive variance of a mean difference is multiplied by one plus the fold count times the test-to-train ratio. The corrected variance is never below the naive one and the inflation grows without bound in the fold count.
  • With a thousand folds at a ratio of one quarter the inflation is 251, the standard error grows by 15.84, and about four folds’ worth of independent evidence remain. The program’s nine wins became three under it, with seventeen indeterminate.

Conditions are curated in entries.toml rather than read from a record.

naive Bayes instrument

DefinitionA classifier that multiplies one-dimensional likelihoods and adds their logs, so that each feature's contribution is the same whatever the others are and it cannot read an interaction. Chapter 6.
ExampleTwo features with likelihood ratios 3 and 2 give a combined ratio of 6, whatever the other features are.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id naive-bayes, kind instrument.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • A classifier that multiplies one-dimensional likelihoods and adds their logs. The log of the product is the sum of the logs, the log odds add across features, and one feature’s contribution is the same whatever the others are, so the score has no interaction terms and its Hessian is diagonal.
  • What naive Bayes cannot read is the interaction, which is a limit of the model class rather than a direction in its kernel, and its read operator is still not diagonal in general because two sensitivities can rise and fall together across rows.
Prior artnone recorded

nearest neighbour concept

DefinitionA row at minimal distance from a query. A strictly increasing transform of the distance names the same nearest neighbours, so the classifier reads the distance's order and nothing else. Chapter 6. Also k-nearest.
ExampleAmong rows at distances 0.9, 0.4, and 1.2 from a query, the second is the nearest, under any increasing rescaling of the distances.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id nearest-neighbour, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • A row at minimal distance from a query under a chosen distance. A strictly increasing transform of the distance names the same nearest neighbours, so a nearest-neighbour classifier reads the distance’s order and nothing else, a row is its own nearest neighbour, and two nearest neighbours sit at the same distance.
  • Under Euclidean distance the classifier reads every standardized coordinate equally and under cosine it reads the angle, so it inherits the distance’s quotient, and the rows that appear in many neighbour lists are the hubs.

neighbourhood graph concept

DefinitionA graph on a dataset that joins each row to its k nearest rows, or to every row within a radius. Chapter 0 section 0.10. Also k-nearest.
ExampleA 5-nearest-neighbour graph on 1000 rows has 5000 out-edges, five from each row.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id neighbourhood-graph, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 0.20.

Assumptions and scope
  • A graph on a dataset that joins each row to its k nearest rows, or to every row within a radius. Every node of a k-nearest graph has out-degree k, the mutual neighbours of a node are at most k, and being mutual neighbours is symmetric.
  • As the graph grows on a manifold its low Laplacian eigenvectors converge to the smoothest functions on the manifold, so the embedding becomes a picture of the manifold, and the hubs of the graph are a property of the queries that built it.

Nine-dimension moral chart concept

DefinitionThe canonical chart of the moral manifold. A generic point has nine coordinates, one per cell of a grid of three ethical scopes (individual, relational, collective) by three epistemic modes (what matters, who decides, what we know). Lower strata may have fewer active dimensions.
ExampleThree scopes times three modes give 3 x 3 = 9 cells, and Rights and Duties is the cell Relational by What Matters. The volume’s measured effective rank is 5.19 of 8 validated axes, so the nine are not nine independent measured coordinates.
VolumeGeometric Ethics, Volume 2 of the Geometric Series; entry id nine-dimension-moral-chart, kind concept.
StatusAppendix F lists Definition 5.2 as a Modeling Axiom, and the ledger row GE-DEF-5-2 is exploratory. The ledger row GE-PURITY-COMPLETENESS, the claim that the nine form a complete basis, has class refuted. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The volume calls the nine a canonical engineering chart chosen for coverage and audit. It does not claim nine is the unique or minimal basis.
  • The completeness claim carried its own falsification condition and the volume reports that the condition is met. Identity attack passed a preregistered gate as a tenth axis, and purity and loyalty also passed a gate.
  • Measured on text, four learned axes do no better than one general-valence channel, and the eight validated axis scores have effective rank 5.19 of 8, below the six the section expected.
  • The rights-and-duties axis could not be learned as a graded score. The volume now treats rights as a hand-specified hard constraint, not a measured coordinate.

nine dimensions of the economic decision manifold concept

DefinitionThe nine coordinates on which the volume scores an economic state. No Escape Theorem result

DefinitionFor an agent whose pipeline satisfies four requirements (mandatory canonicalization, evaluation grounded in physical observables, complete audit, and strong external verification), relative to the declared grounding and transformation group, a re-description that preserves the grounded values leaves the evaluated output unchanged, and an output that violates the constraints is blocked or flagged by audit.
ExampleIf x and x’ describe the same situation, the canonicalizer gives C(x) = C(x’). The evaluation reads only the grounded values of the canonical form, so it returns the same output for both, and renaming alone changes nothing.
VolumeGeometric Ethics, Volume 2 of the Geometric Series; entry id no-escape-theorem, kind result.
StatusTagged Theorem (conditional on Req. 1 to 4) in the text and Conditional Theorem in Appendix F. Ledger row GE-THM-18-1 has class exploratory. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The theorem is conditional on Requirements 1 to 4 and on an adequate grounding. It is as strong as those premises.
  • It blocks cognitive escape routes only. Physical attacks such as sensor spoofing and hardware tampering, and an incomplete grounding, are outside its scope.
  • The volume reports that a version of the I-EIP monitor it proposes for verification failed three sealed preregistrations. It calls that requirement of its architecture an engineering target, not a verified component.
  • Averaging over paraphrases met a preregistered invariance bar on natural rewordings only. Euphemistic rewrites of flagged content still passed, so the volume says this is not adversarial robustness.

No Escape Theorem for Educational AI result

DefinitionAn AI system working on the learner manifold is bound by its structure in four ways. non-commutativity of cooking operations concept

DefinitionCooking operations are operators on flavor space, and in general their order matters. For searing $S$ and braising $B$, $S(B(\mathbf{f}_0)) \neq B(S(\mathbf{f}_0))$. The commutator $[S, B] = SB - BS$ is zero exactly when two operations can be freely reordered. Sequenced operations form a non-abelian monoid.
ExampleLet one step double a number, \(D(x) = 2x\), and another add one, \(A(x) = x + 1\). Then \(D(A(1)) = 4\) and \(A(D(1)) = 3\), so the two orders differ by 1. Two doublings commute. The operators are illustrative stand-ins, not the volume’s.
VolumeGeometric Gastronomy, Volume 12 of the Geometric Series; entry id cooking-non-commutativity, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, with no gastronomy instrument evaluated by the series' admission filter (xbse) and the nearest evaluated perceptual domains, aesthetics and music, rated inadmissible to medium. Its claims are to be read as theory at licensed strength and not as validated measurement, and the chapters tag each statement as a modeling axiom, empirical, a conjecture or a theorem. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Tagged a modeling axiom. The comparison of sear-then-braise with braise-then-sear is qualitative.
  • The structure is a monoid and not a group, since most cooking operations have no inverse.
  • Mixing alone is addition and commutes. The volume says salting and resting roughly commute.
  • In the recipe graph, operations on different branches commute freely. Order matters only along a single path.

normal distribution concept

DefinitionThe bell-shaped distribution with mean mu and standard deviation sigma, with about 68 percent of its mass within one standard deviation, 95 within two, and 99.7 within three, and 1.96 the multiplier for exactly 95. Averages of many independent variables are close to it. Primer S, equation S.8. Also normal approximation, normally distributed.
ExampleA mean with standard error 0.8 has the 95 percent interval plus or minus 1.568.

No Scalar Is Gauge-Invariant (Proposition 3.5) result

DefinitionNo scalar evaluation of a communicative act can be at once invariant under the communication gauge group, sensitive to differences in content, and computable from the signal alone. Any two of the three properties can hold together.
ExampleA semantic distance read off the content coordinate is invariant and content-sensitive, and it needs the content, which the signal alone does not give. An n-gram overlap score is computable from the signal and content-sensitive, and it changes under paraphrase.
VolumeGeometric Communication, Volume 7 of the Geometric Series; entry id signal-scalar-gauge-trilemma, kind result.
StatusA proposition with a proof sketch. The volume gives no full proof and no machine-checked proof. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The argument assumes that different signals can express the same content and that the same signal can arise in different languages, so a function of the signal alone cannot separate content classes.
  • Invariance with content sensitivity is obtained by projecting onto the content manifold, which needs access to the content. Content sensitivity with computability from the signal is what standard metrics have, without invariance.
  • The chapter names three ways to approximate invariance. They are parallel data, structured evaluation, and geometric features invariant under a subgroup.
Prior artnone recorded

nuisance concept

DefinitionThe directions of the data a consumer cannot distinguish, the kernel of its read operator. Chapter 1.
ExampleFor the consumer x1 + x2, the direction (1, −1) is nuisance: moving along it changes nothing.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id nuisance, kind concept.
Statusmeasures [predicted]. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The nuisance is the kernel of the workload-averaged read operator, the set of directions unread at almost every row of that workload, since the kernel of the average is the intersection of the local kernels.
  • For a nonlinear consumer a null direction can turn with the row, so the nuisance of the average is not a global equivalence of inputs, and cosine similarity’s radial direction is the case.
  • A transform is safe when the reader it produces still resolves the read subspace, and discretization is safe only when the values it merges differ in nuisance directions.
Prior artnone recorded

null model instrument

DefinitionA version of the data with the structure under test removed and everything else kept, the right comparison for any measured statistic. Chapter 0 section 0.9.
ExampleShuffling the labels 1000 times and rescoring gives the null distribution the measured score is compared against.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id null-model, kind instrument.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 0.17.

Assumptions and scope
  • A version of the data with the structure under test removed and everything else kept. A label permutation keeps every class size and the bag of scores, so any statistic that reads only class sizes or only scores is unchanged by it, and only a statistic that reads the pairing between score and label can move.
  • That is what makes the permuted statistic the right comparison, and the excess over the null mean is the number a chapter reports. A number without its null is not yet a finding, and the drift claim that lost half its size to a paired null is the ledger’s case.

null space concept

DefinitionThe set of vectors a matrix sends to zero, also called the kernel, the directions the matrix cannot see. Its dimension plus the rank is the number of columns. Primer L, equation L.7. Also null vector.
ExampleRows (1, 2) and (2, 4) send (2, -1) to zero, so the null space is the line of multiples of (2, -1), and 1 + 1 is the 2 columns.

nutritional feasible set and the geometric diet concept

DefinitionThe nutritional feasible set $\mathcal{C}$ is the convex polytope of intake vectors with every nutrient between its lower requirement and its upper limit, $\ell_k \le n_k \le u_k$. The geometric diet set is the set of diets whose nutrition lies in $\mathcal{C}$ and whose flavor lies within $\varepsilon$ of the hedonic manifold.
ExampleWith two nutrients bounded by 50 to 100 and by 20 to 40, the intake (60, 30) is feasible and (60, 45) is not. In the volume’s figures Stigler’s hand solution of 39.93 dollars exceeds the simplex optimum of 39.69 by 0.24 dollars.
VolumeGeometric Gastronomy, Volume 12 of the Geometric Series; entry id geometric-diet-set, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, with no gastronomy instrument evaluated by the series' admission filter (xbse) and the nearest evaluated perceptual domains, aesthetics and music, rated inadmissible to medium. Its claims are to be read as theory at licensed strength and not as validated measurement, and the chapters tag each statement as a modeling axiom, empirical, a conjecture or a theorem. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Both sets are tagged modeling axioms. The palatability and nutritional-quality scalars of Section 11.2 are defined and not measured.
  • Optimizing one scalar over the polytope lands on a vertex. The volume’s case is Stigler’s diet problem, with nine nutrients and 77 foods, costing 39.93 dollars a year by hand and 39.69 by the simplex method, in 1939 dollars.
  • That the diet set is nonempty is argued from traditional cuisines. That seasoning moves are cheap in nutrition and make the problem locally tractable is tagged a conjecture.
  • Both sets differ from person to person. The volume conjectures that there is no universal optimal diet.
Prior artStigler's diet problem (1945) and linear programming over a convex polytope.

Objective hijacking concept

DefinitionA system exhibits objective hijacking when its effective objective is a mixture $(1-\alpha) f_{nom} + \alpha f_{hijack}$ of its nominal objective and a substitute, with hijacking parameter alpha between 0 and 1. For sycophancy the nominal objective seeks truth and the substitute seeks approval.
ExampleWith alpha = 0.25, a nominal objective of 0.8 and a substitute objective of 0.4, the effective objective is 0.75 times 0.8 plus 0.25 times 0.4, which is 0.6 plus 0.1, or 0.7.
VolumeGeometric AI, Volume 11 of the Geometric Series; entry id objective-hijacking, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status block of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, whose alignment thesis is theory at licensed strength and not validated measurement. It adds that no alignment instrument has been evaluated under the xbse admission filter, and the front matter says that ARIA, the system whose numbers fill the chapter tables, is fictional. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The volume reads alpha off wrong-flip rates that it attributes to the Measuring AGI benchmarks of Geometric Cognition. It runs no experiment of its own.
  • The printed values of alpha disagree for one model. Chapter 6 gives about 0.73 for Gemini 2.5 Flash beside a wrong-flip rate of 56%, and Theorem 12.1 gives 0.56 for the same model.
  • The substitution is said to be undetectable by a scalar satisfaction reward because the difference between truth and approval lies in that reward’s kernel. It shows only when the user’s stated opinion diverges from the truth.

observer concept

DefinitionA consumer, its output metric, and its budget, written as the triple in equation 1.1. Naming all three is what every later chapter checks. Also observer triple, the observer.
ExampleA cosine ranker with rank order as its metric and 1000 candidates as its budget is one observer.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id observer, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 1.1.

Assumptions and scope
  • An observer is a consumer, its output metric, and its budget. The consumer and the local geometry of its output metric determine the read operator. The budget bounds what of it can be measured and used and changes it only by changing the consumer.
  • Two consumers with the same read operator on the same workload share a read geometry and are not thereby the same observer, since the consumer stays part of the triple and a sign change reverses every ranking.
  • The output metric is a loss on the consumer’s output. Where it has a local quadratic representation, that local geometry enters the read operator. A dataset-level loss has none, and the read operator is then taken on the score with the identity geometry.
Prior artThe observer triple extends the active-subspace matrix with an output metric, a budget, and an audit discipline.
Evidencegeometric-observation/chapters/ch04_the_observer_triple.md:9-60, geometric-observation/OBSERVATION.md:1-10, geometric-observation/chapters/ch04_the_observer_triple.md:60-135, lean/DataMiningAsObservation/ReadOperator.lean

Witness: the reader’s share of a perturbation falls when the flow’s scale crosses the reader’s budget, after the gradient has grown and on regular flows too; shock formation is one way for the flow’s scale to cross it, not the only one, and a budgeted reader sees it later than the gradient does; the classical extrapolation of the inverse gradient is exact for inviscid Burgers and nothing leads it. Witness: coverage moves the family’s error between the heavy tails at d = 256 and the light-tailed clouds at d = 512 and does not remove it; the pilot recorded before the run that the family, not the set, is the limit, and the run confirmed it; the largest errors of every law of the track sit where the hubness skewness exceeds 12. Absorbed by: declaration. Revision: not another discovery set: a D2v7 changes the target (Poisson hub excess or tail share instead of skewness) or the functional shape, and is a new family and a new registration.
  • OD:world-transfer, transfer of a law frozen on synthetic worlds to embedding corpora, ANN corpora, and dynamical state spaces without retuning. Claim: With full-dimensional clouds at d = 384 and 512 in the discovery set under the log hub-excess target, the frozen law log(excess) = -0.950 - 0.010 / hill_rk + 0.219 log(d_eff) + 0.366 sqrt(id_twonn) predicts hubness on the bracketed clouds, on a cube one step beyond, on the heavy tails, on fresh real slices and at larger N, and beats the nominal law, the chance level and the frozen D2v7 law. experiments/DISCOVERY-TRACK.md, D2v8 record; experiments/OD/D2v8/grade.json. Boundary: the clouds beyond d = 256 all inside the limit and better than D2v7 (cube at d = 448 0.53, Gaussian at d = 512 0.50, cube at d = 640 0.65 against 0.73); real slices 0.14 to 0.24, the best of the track; heavy tails inside the limit but worse than D2v7 on every world (t with 4 degrees at d = 256 0.25 against 0.14); Laplace at N = 12000 at 0.96 outside 0.73; the unseen ball at d = 384 at 1.44, outside and worse than chance; pooled over the transfer groups the frozen D2v7 law at 0.44 beats the law’s 0.47, the fail clause. Witness: coverage of the clouds beyond d = 256 moves the excess family’s error onto the heavy tails and the ball, the sign D2v6 found for the skewness family at about a third of the size; the first law to take a neighbour-distance tail variable misreads the lightest-tailed family, the uniform ball, where the reciprocal Hill term is largest; the D2v7 law, frozen without the clouds, stands as the track’s law. Absorbed by: declaration. Revision: not registered: a change of shape, a term carrying the dimension and the neighbour-distance tail together rather than either alone, is the one repair of D2v6’s list not yet tried; D2v7’s law is the standing law until a registration beats it on the transfer groups.
  • OD:singular-transition, approach to a singularity of the observed dynamics, the periodic Burgers equation carried to shock formation, against a regular two-dimensional flow as the control. Claim: Fourth version: D5v3’s claim with the control bar taken per control, each two-dimensional control’s read fractions collapsing no more tightly on B over its own front wavenumber than on B alone. experiments/DISCOVERY-TRACK.md, D5v4 record; experiments/OD/D5v4/grade.json. Boundary: both controls under the fail line: scaled over unscaled median bin IQR 0.56 (gradient up a third, front wavenumber 3.2 to 4.1) and 0.22 (gradient up two percent, 1.8 to 2.2), against a bar of 0.75 and a fail clause of 0.5; the Burgers worlds at 0.44 and 0.46 on the same draw; convergence 0.012 to 0.095 against 0.11 and the collapse bars held. Witness: the unscaled null takes one value per budget, so each of its bins holds a budget’s whole time series; dividing by any scale that drifts in time spreads that series across bins and lowers the within-bin scatter by construction; the collapse measure is not specific to the forming front, and the readings of D5v2 and D5v3 that it is are withdrawn. Absorbed by: declaration. Revision: a null that is not degenerate, a wrong scale with the same time dependence; a change of the null and so of the claim; not registered.

operating point concept

DefinitionThe row at which a consumer is read, or the threshold at which a classifier is scored. A probe pays 2d evaluations for one. Chapter 0 section 0.5 and chapter 11 section 11.7.
ExampleA probe at one row with 16 directions spends 32 calls at that one operating point.

Defining equation

Book equation 0.8.

Assumptions and scope
  • The row at which a consumer is read, or the threshold at which a classifier is scored. A central-difference probe pays two evaluations per coordinate for one operating point, and raising a classifier’s threshold can only shrink the set it calls positive.
  • Whether many cheaper operating points can average their way back to the population operator was measured within a budget range and not proved, and the cliff at k equal to d does not soften for a probe confined to the directions it chooses.

orthogonal concept

DefinitionOf two vectors, having dot product zero. The squared length of a sum of orthogonal vectors is the sum of the squared lengths. Chapter 0 section 0.1. Also orthonormal.
Example(1, 0) and (0, 1) are orthogonal, and the squared length of their sum is 1 + 1 = 2.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id orthogonal, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 0.1.

Assumptions and scope
  • Of two vectors, having dot product zero. The relation is symmetric, survives rescaling, holds between any vector and zero, the squared length of a sum of orthogonal vectors is the sum of the squared lengths, and the residual of a projection is orthogonal to the direction projected on.
  • A linear classifier’s nuisance is everything orthogonal to its weight vector, and the eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix with distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal, so the read subspace and the nuisance split every row.

outer product concept

DefinitionThe matrix whose entry in row i and column j is the product of a vector's i-th and j-th coordinates, of rank at most one and positive semidefinite for a vector with itself. Chapter 0 section 0.5.
Example(1, 2) with itself gives the matrix with rows (1, 2) and (2, 4), which has rank one.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id outer-product, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 0.9.

Assumptions and scope
  • The matrix whose entry in row i and column j is the product of the i-th and j-th coordinates of a vector. Its action on any vector is a multiple of the vector it was built from, it has rank at most one, and the outer product of a vector with itself is positive semidefinite.
  • The read operator is the weighted mean of the outer product of the sensitivity with itself, and a linear classifier’s read operator is one outer product scaled by how steep the score is.

outlier concept

DefinitionA row the reader cannot place. The statistical detector calls a row an outlier when its distance from the mean in units of spread passes a threshold, and no more than one over the threshold squared of the weight can. Chapter 10. Also z-score.
ExampleA row 3.6 spreads from the mean is an outlier at threshold 3, and by Chebyshev at most one ninth of the weight lies past 3 spreads.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id outlier, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • A row the reader cannot place. The statistical detector scores a row by its distance from the mean in units of spread, which is zero at the mean, unchanged when data, mean, and spread are rescaled and shifted together, and past a threshold t exactly when the row lies more than t spreads from the mean. By Chebyshev the weight of rows beyond t is at most the mean squared score over t squared.
  • The four detector families read different coordinates, distance from the mean, distance to neighbours, density relative to neighbours, and cluster membership, and the observer’s outliers, the anti-hubs, are the rows no detector of the data alone can see.
Prior artnone recorded

output metric concept

DefinitionThe rule by which a consumer's mistakes are scored, the second element of an observer. Chapter 1.
ExampleClassifiers with one and three false positives against three and one false negatives tie on accuracy and split on any cost matrix.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id output-metric, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The rule by which a consumer’s mistakes are scored, the second element of an observer. A consumer and its negation have the same read operator and reverse every comparison, so the read operator alone does not fix the observer, and two cost matrices score the same pair of classifiers in opposite orders, so naming the output metric is naming what a downstream mistake is.
  • A dataset-level loss, accuracy, F1, a rank correlation, or dollars lost is not a local geometry on the score and cannot be inserted into the read-operator formula. Each interestingness measure of chapter 5 and each fairness metric of chapter 14 is an output metric, right for some consumer and wrong for others.

Overton window as geodesic constraint concept

DefinitionA connected, bounded subset $W$ of the preference manifold. Positions inside it cost nothing, and a position outside pays a penalty equal to a coefficient times the squared manifold distance to $W$. A trajectory is Overton-admissible when it stays inside the window of its time.
ExampleWith penalty coefficient 2, a position 3 manifold units outside the window costs \(2 \times 3^2 = 18\), and a position inside costs 0. If the geodesic between two positions has length 4 and the shortest path inside the window has length 6, the Overton cost of the path is 2.
VolumeGeometric Politics, Volume 10 of the Geometric Series; entry id overton-window, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments, and says a political-argument instrument is plausible but has not been built or gated. District 7, the source of nearly every number in the volume, is a fictional district, and Chapter 18 says precise estimation of the manifold needs larger and richer datasets than currently exist. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The boundary is a gradient and not a wall. The quadratic penalty and its coefficient are posited.
  • The window moves. The volume names four forces, which are elite adoption, crisis events, generational replacement and media amplification.
  • The Overton cost of a constrained path is its length minus the length of the unconstrained geodesic. It is zero when the geodesic stays inside the window.
  • The shapes given for the American and Scandinavian windows and for District 7 over three decades are descriptive.
Prior artThe Overton window of Joseph Overton, usually drawn as an interval on the left-right axis.
Evidencegeometric-politics/manuscript/part_iii/ch10_overton_window.md:26-32, geometric-politics/manuscript/part_iii/ch10_overton_window.md:48-54

ExampleScoring both arms on the same 40 documents pairs the comparison, and the difference’s variance drops when the arms covary.

pairwise interaction matrix concept

DefinitionLet $\Delta_i$ be the rise in error from removing dimension i alone. The pairwise interaction $\Phi_{ij}$ is the rise from removing both i and j, minus $\Delta_i + \Delta_j$. A positive value marks a redundant pair, each standing in for the other. A negative value marks a complementary pair, each needing the other.
ExampleIn the volume’s illustration, two copies of one signal cost 0 to remove singly and 1 to remove together, so the interaction is 1 - 0 = +1. Two halves of an exclusive-or cost 1 each and 1 together, so it is 1 - 2 = -1.
VolumeGeometric Methods, Volume 1 of the Geometric Series; entry id pairwise-interaction-matrix, kind concept.
StatusA definition. The identities of Section 12.4.2 are proved and checked symbolically in `formal/matlab/volume_checks.m`, and the tables of Chapter 12 are posited. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • The matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal and costs 1 + n + n(n-1)/2 evaluations for n dimensions.
  • Ablation from the full model is blind to redundant pairs, and adding dimensions one at a time is blind to complementary pairs.
  • The two identities of Section 12.4.2 that tie the matrix to the gains of a build-up sequence hold exactly only when the evaluation function has no interactions above second order.
  • The sign convention was corrected in the November 2026 review. The matrix printed in Section 12.2.2 is hypothetical.
Prior artnone recorded
Evidencegeometric-methods/chapters/chapter-12-compositional-testing.md:76-94

paraphrase class concept

DefinitionA set of rewordings of one input that preserve its meaning. A decision is invariant to re-description when it does not move across the class. Chapter 14. Also paraphrase, re-description, rewording.
ExampleThe sentences ‘the row is stale’ and ‘the row is out of date’ land in one paraphrase class for the encoder.
BookData Mining as Observation, draft 0.3, commit bccca4f; entry id paraphrase-class, kind concept.
Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.

Assumptions and scope
  • A set of rewordings of one input that preserve its meaning. A verdict is invariant to re-description when it does not move across the class, and the ratio of equation 14.3 measures the movement under rewording over the spread between inputs. It is nonnegative, zero exactly when no item’s score moves, and at most one half exactly when the movement is at most half the spread.
  • The measured ratios, 0.407 falling to 0.219 on sixty items and 0.482 to 0.301 under back-translation, with three of six gold items still flipping, are the program’s numbers, and the items that flip are routed to escalation.

Pareto dominance concept

DefinitionA configuration dominates another when it is no worse on every objective and strictly better on at least one. Two configurations of which neither dominates the other are mutually non-dominated, and the non-dominated set is the Pareto frontier.
ExampleWith two objectives to minimize, (2, 3) dominates (2, 4), and neither of (1, 5) and (3, 2) dominates the other.
VolumeGeometric Methods, Volume 1 of the Geometric Series; entry id pareto-dominance, kind concept.
StatusA definition. Appendix C proves in writing that dominance is a strict partial order (Theorem C.7), and its Corollary C.7.1 was restated in the November 2026 review. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Every objective has a direction fixed in advance. The volume minimizes all of them.
  • Dominance is a partial order. It ranks nothing inside the frontier, and a choice there needs a stated preference between the objectives.
  • The frontier tables of Chapter 8 are posited illustrations. In the recorded run of Chapter 19 the frontier had two points, and one of them was a lucky draw on the test set.
Prior artPareto efficiency in economics and the non-dominated sorting of multi-objective optimization.
Evidencegeometric-methods/chapters/chapter-08-pareto-optimization.md:14-20
Reviewednot yet reviewed; generated 2026-11-25 from records at the commits on the provenance page.

pedagogical heuristic and its admissibility concept

DefinitionThe pedagogical heuristic $h_T(x)$ is the teacher's estimate of the geodesic distance from the student's state x to the nearest point of the goal region. It is admissible when $h_T(x)$ is at most that distance for every x, and epsilon-admissible when it exceeds the distance by at most a small epsilon.
ExampleIf the true distance to the goal is 10, an estimate of 8 is admissible. An estimate of 10.5 is not admissible and is epsilon-admissible for epsilon equal to 1. An estimate of 13 is neither.
VolumeGeometric Education, Volume 9 of the Geometric Series; entry id pedagogical-heuristic-admissibility, kind concept.
StatusThe README's epistemic-status note of 2026-07-14 calls this volume a posited framework, speculative theory awaiting instruments. No education-domain instrument has been evaluated by the series' admission filter, and Chapter 18 states that the six predictions of Section 16.3 have not been tested and that no method for estimating the learner metric has been validated at scale. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equationnone
Assumptions and scope
  • Theorem 6.1 states that A* search with an admissible heuristic finds the learner geodesic. The volume gives it as a direct instantiation of the A* optimality theorem of Geometric Reasoning.
  • With an epsilon-admissible heuristic the teaching path is within epsilon of optimal.
  • The volume’s prose reads the admissible case as a teacher who never judges a student ready too early, and the inadmissible case, written \(h_T(x) > d(x, G) + \epsilon\), as a teacher who overestimates readiness. The inequality and the prose should be read together.
  • The mapping of master, competent and miscalibrated teachers onto the three grades is posited. No teacher’s heuristic has been measured.
Prior artAdmissible heuristics for A* search, after Hart, Nilsson and Raphael (1968). The volume ties the calibration of the heuristic to Shulman's pedagogical content knowledge (1986).

percentile concept

DefinitionThe value below which a given fraction of the rows fall. The fraction at or below a value is nondecreasing in the value. Chapter 11 section 11.3.
ExampleAmong 100 sorted ratios, the 97.5th over the 2.5th percentile is the rank certificate’s percentile setting.

Statusno ledger row names this entry. Corrections: none recorded.
Defining equation

Book equation 11.2.

Assumptions and scope
  • The value below which a given fraction of the rows fall. The fraction at or below a value is nonnegative, at most one, nondecreasing in the value, one at or above the largest row and zero below the smallest, and an upper percentile over a lower one is at least one.
  • The rank certificate’s percentile setting reads the 97.5 over 2.5 percentile ratio as a robust estimate where the strict setting reads the max over min, and the anti-hub gate reads the fifth percentile of recall.

per-channel quantizer instrument

DefinitionA quantizer that chooses a scale per coordinate. Chapter 11. Also per-channel.

permutation test concept

DefinitionA test that computes the p-value by reassigning the labels under the null, every way or a few thousand random ways, and counting the fraction of statistics at least as extreme as the observed. It needs no assumption about the shape of the data, and the sample size fixes the smallest p-value it can give. Primer S, equation S.15. Also permut.
ExampleGroups (8, 9) and (4, 5) have six reassignments, two with a difference of at least 4 in size, so the two-sided p-value is one third.
